metadata.title: Ahlfors-regular distances on the Heisenberg group without biLipschitz pieces
metadata.authors: Enrico Le Donne, Sean Li, Tapio Rajala

nodes.name: minimal in looking down
nodes.statement: A space $X$ is \emph{mimimal} in looking down if every space $Y$ on which $X$ looks down is look-down equivalent to $X$.
differentia: every space $Y$ on which $X$ looks down is look-down equivalent to $X$

nodes.name: Which BPI spaces are minimal in looking down?
nodes.statement: The partial ordering of BPI spaces raises the interesting question of what are the possible minimal spaces in this ordering.
nodes.statement_short: Classify the spaces that are minimal for the looking-down partial order on BPI spaces.

nodes.name: Look-down equivalence does not imply BPI equivalence (Laakso)
nodes.statement: However, Laakso has shown that the converse is not true in general \cite{laakso-bpi}.
assumptions: BPI equivalence of spaces $X$ and $Y$ implies that $X$ and $Y$ are \emph{look-down equivalent}
conclusions: the converse is not true in general

nodes.name: Kirchheim's theorem (Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down)
nodes.statement: For example, from the result of Kirchheim \cite{Kirchheim} we know that Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down.
assumptions: from the result of Kirchheim \cite{Kirchheim}
conclusions: Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down

nodes.name: Quantitative Kirchheim theorem (large biLipschitz piece)
nodes.statement: A quantitative version of Kirchheim's theorem was later given in \cite{Schul_BiLipschitz_Decomposition} in which it was shown that if a map $f : [0,1]^n \to X$ has positive Hausdorff $n$-content, then it has a quantitatively large biLipschitz piece.
nodes.statement_short: A map from $[0,1]^n$ with positive Hausdorff $n$-content has a quantitatively large biLipschitz piece.
assumptions: if a map $f : [0,1]^n \to X$ has positive Hausdorff $n$-content
conclusions: it has a quantitatively large biLipschitz piece

nodes.name: Problem 11.15 of David-Semmes / Question 22 of Heinonen-Semmes
nodes.statement: David and Semmes asked in Problem 11.15 of \cite{davsem} if the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ is also minimal in looking down, when equipped with sub-Riemannian distances, also called Carnot-Carath\'eodory distances. This was also asked as Question 22 of \cite{Heinonen_Semmes}.
nodes.statement_short: Is the subRiemannian Heisenberg group minimal in looking down?
nodes.origin_citation: David & Semmes, Problem 11.15; Heinonen & Semmes, Question 22

nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 (the subRiemannian Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down)
nodes.statement: The subRiemannian Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down.
assumptions: The subRiemannian Heisenberg group
conclusions: is not minimal in looking down

nodes.name: countably $n$-rectifiable metric measure space
nodes.statement: Recall that a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is countably $n$-rectifiable if there exist a countable set of Borel subsets $A_i \subseteq \R^n$ and Lipschitz maps $f : A_i \to X$ such that $\mu\left(X \backslash \bigcup_i f(A_i) \right) = 0$ and $\mu \ll \H^n$ where $\H^n$ is the Hausdorff $n$-measure.
nodes.statement_short: A metric measure space is countably $n$-rectifiable if it is covered up to measure zero by Lipschitz images of Borel subsets of $\R^n$, with $\mu \ll \H^n$.
differentia: there exist a countable set of Borel subsets $A_i \subseteq \R^n$ and Lipschitz maps $f : A_i \to X$

nodes.name: Kirchheim's biLipschitz decomposition of rectifiable pieces
nodes.statement: It was shown in \cite{Kirchheim} that, by further countably decomposing each $f(A_i)$ if necessary, one may assume that each $f_i$ is biLipschitz.
assumptions: by further countably decomposing each $f(A_i)$ if necessary
conclusions: one may assume that each $f_i$ is biLipschitz

nodes.name: $\mathbb H$-rectifiable
nodes.statement: One can easily create a definition of being $\mathbb H$-rectifiable by letting each $A_i$ be a Borel subset of the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ and setting $n = 4$, the Hausdorff dimension of $\mathbb H$.
differentia: letting each $A_i$ be a Borel subset of the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ and setting $n = 4$

nodes.name: Lipschitz rectifiability is strictly weaker than biLipschitz rectifiability in $\mathbb H$
nodes.statement: However, we now see that there exists a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ with positive Hausdorff 4-measure that is the Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ but is not the countable union of biLipschitz images of subsets of $\mathbb H$. Thus, ``Lipschitz rectifiability'' is strictly weaker than ``biLipschitz rectifiability'' when using the Heisenberg geometry.
nodes.statement_short: In Heisenberg geometry, Lipschitz rectifiability is strictly weaker than biLipschitz rectifiability.
assumptions: there exists a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ with positive Hausdorff 4-measure that is the Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ but is not the countable union of biLipschitz images of subsets of $\mathbb H$
conclusions: ``Lipschitz rectifiability'' is strictly weaker than ``biLipschitz rectifiability'' when using the Heisenberg geometry

nodes.name: Theorem 1.2 (a shortened Ahlfors 4-regular distance on $\mathbb H$)
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathbb H, d_{cc})$ be the subRiemannian Heisenberg group. There exists a distance $d$ on $\mathbb H $ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $d\leq d_{cc}$; \item $(\mathbb H, d)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular; \item if $A\subseteq \mathbb H$ is a subset with $\H^4_{cc}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $d_{cc}$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: There is a distance $d \le d_{cc}$ on $\mathbb H$ that is still Ahlfors 4-regular but biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$ on no set of positive measure.
assumptions: Let $(\mathbb H, d_{cc})$ be the subRiemannian Heisenberg group.
conclusions: $d\leq d_{cc}$
$(\mathbb H, d)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular
if $A\subseteq \mathbb H$ is a subset with $\H^4_{cc}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $d_{cc}$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$

nodes.name: Theorem 1.2 answers Question 24 of Heinonen-Semmes negatively
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} answers Question 24 of \cite{Heinonen_Semmes} negatively (although the same negative answer is provided by the negative answer to Question 22 given by Theorem~\ref{thm:Hnotminimal}).

nodes.name: Lipschitz maps between Carnot groups have biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement: Indeed, one can then use a similar argument as in \cite{Kirchheim}, with inspiration from \cite{pauls}, to show that Lipschitz maps from the Heisenberg group to another Carnot group with positive 4-measure image have biLipschitz pieces. This statement can also be made quantitative as was done in \cite{Meyerson_Lipschitz_biLipschitz,Li-lip-bilip}.
nodes.statement_short: For Carnot-group targets, Lipschitz maps out of $\mathbb H$ with positive 4-measure image do have biLipschitz pieces.
assumptions: Lipschitz maps from the Heisenberg group to another Carnot group with positive 4-measure image
conclusions: have biLipschitz pieces

nodes.name: G.C. David's biLipschitz-piece theorem
nodes.statement: Another situation where Lipschitz maps have biLipschitz pieces is when the spaces are Ahlfors regular, linearly locally contractible topological manifolds and the target has manifold weak tangents, see the work of G.C. David \cite{gcdavid} (this David is not the same David of David-Semmes).
assumptions: the spaces are Ahlfors regular, linearly locally contractible topological manifolds and the target has manifold weak tangents
conclusions: Lipschitz maps have biLipschitz pieces

nodes.name: The space of Theorem 1.2 has neither manifold tangents nor local contractibility
nodes.statement: We note that in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} the constructed space $(\mathbb H, d)$ neither has manifold tangents nor is linearly locally contractible.

nodes.name: Theorem 1.3 (general shortcut theorem in Ahlfors $Q$-regular spaces)
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and $Q>0$. Assume \begin{enumerate} \item $(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular; \item there exists $\lambda\in(0,1)$ such that for all $p\in X$ and all $0 < r < \diam(X)$ there exist $q_1, q_2\in B_\rho (p,r)$ such that $$\rho(q_1, q_2) \geq \lambda r$$ and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \leq \rho (p_1, q_1) + \rho (p_2, q_2), \qquad \forall p_1, p_2 \notin B_\rho (p,r). \end{equation} \end{enumerate} Then there exists a distance $d$ on $X $ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $d\leq \rho$; \item $(X, d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular; \item if $A\subseteq X$ is a subset with $\H^Q_{\rho}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: An Ahlfors $Q$-regular space admitting well-separated shortcut pairs carries a smaller Ahlfors $Q$-regular distance that is biLipschitz to the original on no positive-measure set.
assumptions: Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and $Q>0$.
$(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular
there exists $\lambda\in(0,1)$ such that for all $p\in X$ and all $0 < r < \diam(X)$ there exist $q_1, q_2\in B_\rho (p,r)$ such that $$\rho(q_1, q_2) \geq \lambda r$$
conclusions: $d\leq \rho$
$(X, d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular
if $A\subseteq X$ is a subset with $\H^Q_{\rho}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$

nodes.name: Theorem 1.4 (biLipschitz left-translations force biLipschitz equivalence)
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be a distance on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ such that $d \le d_{cc}$ and $\H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$. Assume that the left translations in $\mathbb H$ are biLipschitz with respect to $d$. Then $d$ and $ d_{cc}$ are biLipschitz equivalent on compact sets.
nodes.statement_short: A distance below $d_{cc}$ with positive $\H^4$ on a $d_{cc}$-ball and biLipschitz left translations is biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$ on compact sets.
assumptions: Let $d$ be a distance on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ such that $d \le d_{cc}$ and $\H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$.
Assume that the left translations in $\mathbb H$ are biLipschitz with respect to $d$.
conclusions: Then $d$ and $ d_{cc}$ are biLipschitz equivalent on compact sets.

nodes.name: Necessity of the assumptions of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: We remark that the assumptions in Theorem~\ref{thm:positiveinvarianttobilip} are necessary. Indeed, if we don't assume $d \le d_{cc}$, then as a counterexample one can take two sub-Riemannian distances on $\mathbb H$ that have two different horizontal bundles. If we don't assume $\H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$, then a counterexample is given by every Riemannian left-invariant distance. Moreover, the distance $\min\{1, d_{cc}\}$ shows that the conclusion of the theorem may not be global.
nodes.statement_short: Dropping $d \le d_{cc}$, dropping $\H^4_d(B_{cc}(0,1))>0$, or asking for a global conclusion all fail.

nodes.name: Kirchheim's metric differentiability theorem
nodes.statement: Kirchheim's result in \cite{Kirchheim} can be stated as the fact that every semi-distance $d$ in $\R^n$ that is smaller than the Euclidean distance is metrically differentiable, i.e., at almost every point its blow-up is a homogeneous semi-distance.
assumptions: every semi-distance $d$ in $\R^n$ that is smaller than the Euclidean distance
conclusions: is metrically differentiable, i.e., at almost every point its blow-up is a homogeneous semi-distance

nodes.name: Metric differentiability on Carnot groups in horizontal directions
nodes.statement: Similarly, by \cite{Pauls01}, we know that on Carnot groups semi-distances smaller than $ d_{cc}$ are metrically differentiable but only in the horizontal directions.
assumptions: on Carnot groups semi-distances smaller than $ d_{cc}$
conclusions: are metrically differentiable but only in the horizontal directions

nodes.name: Kirchheim-Magnani counterexample to metric differentiability
nodes.statement: Regarding non-horizontal directions, from \cite{Kirchheim_Magnani} we know that there is a distance in the Heisenberg group that is a counterexample to metric differentiability, although it is not biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$.
conclusions: there is a distance in the Heisenberg group that is a counterexample to metric differentiability, although it is not biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$

nodes.name: self-similar (semi-)distance
nodes.statement: a (semi-)distance $d$ is {\em self-similar} if there exists some $\lambda>1$ for which $d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q)$, for all $p,q\in \mathbb H $.
differentia: there exists some $\lambda>1$ for which $d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q)$, for all $p,q\in \mathbb H $

nodes.name: blow-up of a distance
nodes.statement: In the following result, by {\em a blow-up} of a distance $d$ we mean any pointwise limit of the functions \[(p_1,p_2)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d( q_j \delta_{\lambda_j} ( p_1), q_j \delta_{\lambda_j} ( p_2)) ,\] as $\lambda_j \to 0$ and $q_j\in \mathbb H $.
nodes.genus: any pointwise limit of the functions

nodes.name: Theorem 1.5 (Failure of Kirchheim-metric differentiation for biLipschitz maps)
nodes.statement: There exist two distances $d_1, d_2$ on $\mathbb H $ that are biLipschitz equivalent to $d_{cc}$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item The distance $d_1$ is left-invariant, but no blow-up of $d_1$ is self-similar. \item No blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant nor self-similar. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: There are two distances biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$ whose blow-ups are never self-similar (and, for $d_2$, never left-invariant).
assumptions: There exist two distances $d_1, d_2$ on $\mathbb H $ that are biLipschitz equivalent to $d_{cc}$
conclusions: The distance $d_1$ is left-invariant, but no blow-up of $d_1$ is self-similar.
No blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant nor self-similar.

nodes.name: Hausdorff $Q$-measure
nodes.statement: We begin by recalling the definition of Hausdorff measures on a metric space $(X,d)$. Let $Q > 0$. Then for $A \subseteq X$, one defines \[ \H^Q_d(A) := \lim_{s \to 0^+} \inf \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^\infty (\diam E_i)^Q : A \subseteq \bigcup_i E_i \text{ an open cover}, \diam(E_i) < s\right\}. \] We say that $\H^Q$ is the Hausdorff $Q$-measure of $(X,d)$. It is known that the Hausdorff $Q$-measure is Borel regular although it may not be locally finite.
nodes.statement_short: $\H^Q_d$ is the usual Hausdorff $Q$-measure, obtained as the $s \to 0^+$ limit of infima of $\sum (\diam E_i)^Q$ over fine open covers.

nodes.name: Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric measure space
nodes.statement: Recall that a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is said to be Ahlfors $Q$-regular if there exists $C \geq 1$ so that \[\frac{1}{C} r^Q \leq \mu(B(x,r)) \leq C r^Q, \qquad \forall x \in X, r < \frac{\diam X}{2}.\]
differentia: there exists $C \geq 1$ so that \[\frac{1}{C} r^Q \leq \mu(B(x,r)) \leq C r^Q, \qquad \forall x \in X, r < \frac{\diam X}{2}.\]

nodes.name: Ahlfors regularity passes to the Hausdorff measure
nodes.statement: We remark that if $(X,d,\mu)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular, then $(X,d,\H^Q)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular.

nodes.name: $C$-conformally biLipschitz map (quasi-similarity)
nodes.statement: A biLipschitz map $f$ between metric spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ is said to be $C$-{\em conformally biLipschitz} with scale factor $\lambda > 0$ if $f$ is $C$-biLipschitz between the metric spaces $(X, \lambda d)$ and $(X',d')$. Another term, coming from Banach space theory, for the same notion is {\em quasi-similarity}.
differentia: $f$ is $C$-biLipschitz between the metric spaces $(X, \lambda d)$ and $(X',d')$
nodes.genus: A biLipschitz map $f$ between metric spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$

nodes.name: BPI (``big pieces of itself'') space
nodes.statement: An Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space $(X,d)$ is said to be a \emph{BPI} (``big pieces of itself'') {\em space} if there exist constants $C \ge 1$ and $\theta > 0$ such that for all $x_1,x_2 \in X$ and $0 < r_1 , r_2 < \diam(X)$ there is a closed set $A \subseteq B(x_1,r_1)$ with $\mathcal{H}^Q(A) \ge \theta r_1^Q$ and if there is a $C$-conformally biLipschitz embedding $f \colon A \to B(x_2,r_2)$ with scale factor $r_2/r_1$.
nodes.statement_short: An Ahlfors $Q$-regular space in which any two balls contain, at definite density, conformally biLipschitz copies of each other.
differentia: there exist constants $C \ge 1$ and $\theta > 0$ such that for all $x_1,x_2 \in X$ and $0 < r_1 , r_2 < \diam(X)$ there is a closed set $A \subseteq B(x_1,r_1)$ with $\mathcal{H}^Q(A) \ge \theta r_1^Q$

nodes.name: BPI equivalence
nodes.statement: Two BPI spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ of the same dimension $Q$ are called \emph{BPI equivalent} if there exist constants $\theta>0$ and $C>0$ such that for each $x \in X$, $x' \in X'$ and radii $0 < R < \diam(X)$, $0 < R' < \diam(X')$ there exist a subset $A \subset B(x,R) \subset X$ with $\H^Q_d(A)\ge \theta R^Q$ and an $C$-conformally biLipschitz embedding $f \colon A \to B(x',R')$ with scale factor $R'/R$.
nodes.statement_short: Two BPI spaces of the same dimension are BPI equivalent if balls in one contain definite-density conformally biLipschitz copies inside balls of the other.
nodes.genus: Two BPI spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ of the same dimension $Q$

nodes.name: looking down / look-down equivalent
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ be BPI metric spaces of Hausdorff dimension $Q$. The space $(X,d)$ is said to \emph{look down on} $(X',d')$ if there is a closed set $A \subset X$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon A \to X'$ such that $f(A)$ has positive Hausdorff $Q$-measure. If also $X'$ looks down on $X$, then $X$ and $X'$ are called \emph{look-down equivalent}.
differentia: there is a closed set $A \subset X$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon A \to X'$ such that $f(A)$ has positive Hausdorff $Q$-measure
nodes.genus: BPI metric spaces of Hausdorff dimension $Q$

nodes.name: Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$
nodes.statement: The Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ is the simply connected Lie group whose Lie algebra is generated by three vectors $X,Y,Z$ with only non-zero relation $[X,Y]=Z$. Via exponential coordinates it can be identified as the manifold $\R^3$ equipped with Lie multiplication: \[ p\cdot q = \left( x_p + x_q, y_p + y_q, z_p + z_q + \frac12 (x_py_q - y_px_q) \right). \]

nodes.name: dilations $\delta_\lambda$ of $\mathbb H$
nodes.statement: For each $\lambda > 0$, the Heisenberg group has an automorphism defined as \begin{equation} \delta_\lambda (x,y,z) := (\lambda x, \lambda y, \lambda^2 z). \end{equation}

nodes.name: homogeneous (semi-)distance
nodes.statement: A left-invariant (semi-)distance $d$ is {\em homogeneous}, with respect to \eqref{hom:dil}, if for all $\lambda>0$ \begin{equation} d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q\in \mathbb H. \end{equation}

differentia: for all $\lambda>0$ \begin{equation} d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q\in \mathbb H. \end{equation}

nodes.name: box norm
nodes.statement: We introduce the {\em box norm} \[ \norm{p} := \max\left\{|x_p|,|y_p|, \sqrt{|z_p|}\right\}. \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: box distance $d_b$
nodes.statement: We define the {\em box distance} as \[ d_b(p,q) := \norm{p^{-1}q}. \]

nodes.name: $d_b$ is a left-invariant homogeneous distance
nodes.statement: Clearly, $d_b$ is left-invariant and it satisfies \eqref{eq:homog:dist}.

nodes.statement: Explicitely, the box distance is \begin{equation} d_b(p_1,p_2) = \max\left\{|x_1-x_2|,|y_1-y_2|, \sqrt{\left|z_1-z_2-\frac12(x_1y_2-x_2y_1)\right|}\right\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Jacobian $J(L)$ of a homomorphism
nodes.statement: Given a homomorphism $L : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$, one can define the Jacobian to be \[ J(L) = \frac{\H^4_{d_b}(L(B_{d_b}(0,1)))}{\H_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,1))}. \]

nodes.name: Pansu differentiability theorem
nodes.statement: Let $f : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to ({\mathbb H},d_b)$ be a Lipschitz map. Pansu proved in \cite{Pansu} that for almost every $x \in {\mathbb H}$ there exists a Lipschitz homomorphism $Df(x) : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$ (the Pansu-derivative of $f$ at $x$) so that \[ Df(x) (g) = \lim_{\lambda \to 0} \delta_{1/\lambda} (f(x)^{-1} f(x \delta_\lambda(g))). \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
nodes.statement_short: A Lipschitz self-map of $\mathbb H$ admits a homomorphism-valued Pansu derivative almost everywhere.
assumptions: Let $f : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to ({\mathbb H},d_b)$ be a Lipschitz map.
conclusions: for almost every $x \in {\mathbb H}$ there exists a Lipschitz homomorphism $Df(x) : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$ (the Pansu-derivative of $f$ at $x$)

nodes.name: Magnani's area formula
nodes.statement: This result was extended to Lipschitz maps whose domains are measurable subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb H$ by Magnani in \cite{magnani-area}. Magnani also used the Pansu-derivative in conjunction with the Jacobian to get the following area formula: \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb H} N(f,A,y) d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(y) = \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x). \end{equation} Here, $N(f,A,y)$ is the multiplicity of $f$ with respect to the set $A$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
nodes.statement_short: Area formula: the multiplicity integral of $f$ equals the integral of the Pansu Jacobian over the domain.
conclusions: \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb H} N(f,A,y) d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(y) = \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x). \end{equation}

nodes.name: cost function
nodes.statement: Given a metric space $(X,\rho)$, a symmetric function $c:X\times X \to [0,\infty)$ such that $c\leq \rho$ will be called a {\em cost function}.

nodes.name: shortcut (flight, tunnel) and the set $\S$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\S$ all those pairs of points $(x,y)\in X\times X$ such that $c(x,y)< \rho(x,y)$ $$\S:=\{ (x,y)\in X\times X\;:\; c(x,y)< \rho(x,y)\}.$$ An element in $\S$ will be called {\em shortcut} (or flight or tunnel).

nodes.name: itinerary and the collection $\I$
nodes.statement: If we have $N\in \N$ and $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N\in X$ then the $N$-tuple ${\bf x} = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ will be called an {\em itinerary} from the extreme points $x_0$ to $x_N$ and we set ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x}):=(x_0,x_N)$ and $\ell({\bf x}) := N$. We will denote by $\I$ the collection of all itineraries in $X$, i.e., $$\I:=\{(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N) \;:\; N\in \N, \,x_j\in X \}.$$

nodes.name: cost of an itinerary
nodes.statement: The {\em cost} of an itinerary ${\bf x}= (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N) \in \I$ is $$c ({\bf x}):= \sum_{i=1}^N c(x_{i-1}, x_i).$$

nodes.name: distance $d$ associated to a cost function
nodes.statement: The distance $d$ associated to the cost function $c$ is defined as \begin{equation} d(x,y): = \inf\{ c ({\bf x}) \;:\; {\bf x} \in \I ,\, {\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(x,y)\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $d(x,y)$ is the infimum of itinerary costs over all itineraries joining $x$ to $y$.
nodes.definiendum: The distance $d$ associated to the cost function $c$

nodes.name: Remark 2.4 ($d$ is a semi-distance, and a distance when dominated below)
nodes.statement: It is not too hard to verify symmetry and the triangle inequality for $d$ and so $d$ is a semi-distance on $X$. If there is another distance $d'$ on $X$ such that \[ d'(x,y) \leq c(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in X, \] then by the triangle inequality for $d'$, we also have that \[ d'(x,y) \leq d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in X, \] and so $d$ is then a distance.
nodes.statement_short: $d$ is always a semi-distance; if some distance $d'$ satisfies $d' \le c$ then $d' \le d$, so $d$ is a distance.

nodes.name: alternating itineraries $\I_A$
nodes.statement: We define the subset of {\it alternating itineraries} as $$\I_A:=\{{\bf x} \in \I \;:\; (x_{j-1},x_{j})\in \S \iff j \text{ even} \}.$$ Colloquially speaking, for each of these itineraries, one walks at every odd step and flies at every even step. Note that we allow for the stationary walks, i.e., the itinerary can have $x_{j-1} = x_{j}$, for some $j$ odd.
nodes.statement_short: Itineraries that walk on odd steps and fly (use a shortcut) on even steps, stationary walks allowed.

nodes.name: level function $L$ of shortcuts
nodes.statement: We shall assign to each shortcut a natural number that we call {\em level} of the shortcut. Namely, a function $L \colon \S \to \N$ will be called a {\em level function}. Larger levels will usually indicate shortcuts over smaller distances.

nodes.name: level function $L_{\bf x}$ of an alternating itinerary
nodes.statement: We can also define the level function of an alternating itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I_A$ as the function \begin{eqnarray*} L_{\bf x} : \{1,\dots,\lfloor N/2 \rfloor \} &\to& \N \\ k &\mapsto& L(x_{2k-1},x_{2k}). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.definiendum: the level function of an alternating itinerary

nodes.name: decreasing-increasing function
nodes.statement: We say that a function $f : \{1,\dots,n\} \to \R$ is {\em decreasing-increasing} if there is some $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ for which $f|_{[1,k]}$ is decreasing and $f|_{[k+1,n]}$ is increasing (both not necessarily strictly monotonically).
differentia: there is some $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ for which $f|_{[1,k]}$ is decreasing and $f|_{[k+1,n]}$ is increasing

nodes.name: itineraries with decreasing-increasing level functions $\I^*$
nodes.statement: We can then define a further subset of itineraries with decreasing-increasing level functions: $$\I^*:=\{{\bf x} \in \I_A \;:\; L_\x \text{ is decreasing-increasing} \}.$$

nodes.name: Inductive construction of the level $n$ shortcuts
nodes.statement: Let $(\alpha_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of real numbers in $(0,1)$ such that $\alpha_n \downarrow 0$. The number $\alpha_n$ will be the ratio of the cost of the level $n$ shortcut compared to the original distance of the shortcut. Let us define the shortcuts one level at a time. We define inductively the level $n$ shortcuts $\S_n \subset X \times X$, for $n \in \N$ as follows. We set $c_E \ge 4$ to be a constant that we now fix. Let $\mathcal{N}_n := \{x_i\}$ be a set of points in \[ X \setminus \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1}\bigcup_{(x,y) \in \S_j} B_\rho(\{x,y\}, 4\lambda^n) \] such that $\rho(x_i,x_j) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and $X \subseteq \bigcup_i B_\rho(x_i,c_E \lambda^n)$. It may be that one could choose $c_E$ so that no such $\mathcal{N}_n$ exists. We show later in Lemma~\ref{lma:constantsexist} that there is always a choice of the constants $\lambda$ and $c_E$ for which the set $\mathcal{N}_n$ exists. Using assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} we select for each $i$ points $q_{i,1}, q_{i,2} \in B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n)$ such that \[ \rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} \] and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \le \rho(p_1,q_{i,1}) + \rho(p_2, q_{i,2}) \qquad \text{for all }p_1,p_2 \notin B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n). \end{equation} Now define the level $n$ shortcuts as \[ \S_n := \{(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2})\,:\, i\} \cup \{(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1})\,:\, i\}, \] their corresponding costs as \[ c(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := c(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := \alpha_n\rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \] and their level as \[ L(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := L(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := n. \] Finally, let \[ \S := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \S_n \] and define $d$ as in \eqref{eq:ddef}.
nodes.statement_short: Level by level, pick a $4\lambda^n$-separated $c_E\lambda^n$-net avoiding earlier shortcuts, attach a shortcut pair inside each net ball with cost $\alpha_n\rho$, and let $d$ be the induced distance.
input: Let $(\alpha_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of real numbers in $(0,1)$ such that $\alpha_n \downarrow 0$.
We set $c_E \ge 4$ to be a constant that we now fix.

nodes.name: Choose the net $\mathcal{N}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N}_n := \{x_i\}$ be a set of points in \[ X \setminus \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1}\bigcup_{(x,y) \in \S_j} B_\rho(\{x,y\}, 4\lambda^n) \] such that $\rho(x_i,x_j) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and $X \subseteq \bigcup_i B_\rho(x_i,c_E \lambda^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a $4\lambda^n$-separated $c_E\lambda^n$-net away from all lower-level shortcut points.

nodes.name: Select the shortcut endpoints
nodes.statement: Using assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} we select for each $i$ points $q_{i,1}, q_{i,2} \in B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n)$ such that \[ \rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} \] and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \le \rho(p_1,q_{i,1}) + \rho(p_2, q_{i,2}) \qquad \text{for all }p_1,p_2 \notin B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Inside each net ball choose $q_{i,1},q_{i,2}$ that are $\lambda^{n+1}$-far apart and satisfy the shortcut inequality.

nodes.name: Define level $n$ shortcuts, costs and levels
nodes.statement: Now define the level $n$ shortcuts as \[ \S_n := \{(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2})\,:\, i\} \cup \{(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1})\,:\, i\}, \] their corresponding costs as \[ c(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := c(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := \alpha_n\rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \] and their level as \[ L(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := L(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrize the chosen pairs into $\S_n$, set their cost to $\alpha_n\rho$ and their level to $n$.

nodes.name: Assemble $\S$ and define $d$
nodes.statement: Finally, let \[ \S := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \S_n \] and define $d$ as in \eqref{eq:ddef}.
nodes.statement_short: Take the union over all levels and let $d$ be the induced shortcut distance.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 (existence of the nets $\mathcal{N}_n$)
nodes.statement: There exists some $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/4)$ depending only on the Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$ such that if we set $\lambda \leq \lambda_0$ and $c_E = 8 + \frac1\lambda$, then we can always find $\mathcal{N}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\lambda$ small enough and $c_E = 8 + 1/\lambda$ the required nets $\mathcal{N}_n$ always exist.
assumptions: There exists some $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/4)$ depending only on the Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$ such that if we set $\lambda \leq \lambda_0$
$c_E = 8 + \frac1\lambda$
conclusions: then we can always find $\mathcal{N}_n$

nodes.name: Choose $\lambda$ small by Ahlfors regularity
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\rho)$ so that $(X,\rho,\mu)$ is Ahlfors regular (one could use $\mu = \H^Q$ for instance). We may suppose by taking $\lambda$ small enough (as we are free to do) and using Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho,\mu)$ that \begin{equation} \mu(B_\rho(x,r/4)) - \mu(B_\rho(y,\lambda r)) - \mu(B_\rho(z, \lambda r)) > 0, \qquad \forall x,y,z \in X, 0 < r < \diam(X). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix an Ahlfors-regular measure and shrink $\lambda$ so that a three-ball measure difference stays positive.

nodes.name: Claim: earlier shortcut points are $2\lambda^{n-1}$-separated
nodes.statement: Let $A = \bigcup_{j < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in \S_j} \{x,y\}$. By the definition of $A$, each $x \in A$ comes with a pair $x' \in A$ such that $(x,x') \in S_l$ for some $l < n$. We claim that \begin{equation} \rho(x,y) \geq 2 \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad \forall y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $A$ to be all earlier shortcut endpoints and claim the separation estimate.

nodes.name: Case $k = l$
nodes.statement: We consider two cases. Suppose first that $k = l$. By the $4\lambda^k$ separation of $\mathcal{N}_k$ we then have \[ \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,x_j^k) - \rho(x,x_i^l) - \rho(y,x_j^k) \ge 4\lambda^k - \lambda^k - \lambda^k = 2\lambda^k \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Same level: use the $4\lambda^k$ separation of $\mathcal{N}_k$.

nodes.name: Case $k \ne l$
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $k \ne l$. By symmetry we may assume $k < l$. Then by construction, $x_i^l \notin B_\rho(y,4\lambda^l)$ and thus \[ \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,y) - \rho(x,x_i^l) \ge 4\lambda^l - \lambda^l = 3\lambda^l \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}. \] Thus \eqref{e:A-spread-out} is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Different levels: the higher-level net point was chosen outside a $4\lambda^l$-ball.

nodes.name: Build the net and estimate the covering radius
nodes.statement: Let $\{x_i\}$ be a maximal $4\lambda^n$-separated net of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$. Let $x \in X$. Suppose there exists $y \in A$ such that $\rho(x,y) < 4\lambda^n$. As $\lambda < 1/4$, we get by \eqref{e:A-spread-out} that the number of balls $\{B_\rho(p,4 \lambda^n)\}_{p \in A}$ that intersect $B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1})$ is at most 2. This, together with \eqref{e:small-lambda}, gives that \[ B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1}) \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n) \neq \emptyset. \] Thus, there exists some $z \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1}) \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$. As $\{x_i\}$ is also a $4\lambda^n$ covering of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$, we get that there exists some $x_i$ such that $\rho(z,x_i) < 4\lambda^n$. Altogether, we get that \[ \rho(x,x_i) \leq \rho(x,y) + \rho(y,z) + \rho(z,x_i) < 4\lambda^n + \lambda^{n-1} + 4 \lambda^n = \left(8 + \frac{1}{\lambda} \right)\lambda^n. \] In the case when $x \notin B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$, we are also done as the set $\{x_i\}$ is a $4\lambda^n$-cover of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal separated net off $A$ and check every point is within $(8+1/\lambda)\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2 (removing a locally maximal shortcut level)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I_A$ and there exists $j \in 2\N-1$ such that $$L(x_{j+2},x_{j+3}) \geq \max(L(x_j,x_{j+1}),L(x_{j+4},x_{j+5})).$$ Then the itinerary ${\bf x}' = (x_0',\dots,x_{N-2}') \in \I_A$ where \[ x_k' = \begin{cases} x_k & k \in \{0,\dots,j+1\}, \\ x_{k+2} & k \in \{j+2,\dots,N-2\}, \end{cases} \] satisfies $\Ext({\bf x}) = \Ext({\bf x}')$ and $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$.
nodes.statement_short: An alternating itinerary with a locally maximal shortcut level can be shortened by two points without increasing cost.
assumptions: Suppose $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I_A$ and there exists $j \in 2\N-1$ such that $$L(x_{j+2},x_{j+3}) \geq \max(L(x_j,x_{j+1}),L(x_{j+4},x_{j+5})).$$
conclusions: satisfies $\Ext({\bf x}) = \Ext({\bf x}')$ and $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Show the flanking points lie outside the ball where the maximal-level shortcut was found, then apply the shortcut inequality to replace the subitinerary.

nodes.name: Reduce to a subitinerary claim
nodes.statement: That $\Ext({\bf x}) = \Ext({\bf x}')$ is obvious from construction. Consider the subitinerary ${\bf y} = (x_{j+1},x_{j+2},x_{j+3},x_{j+4})$. We claim that $c(x_{j+1},x_{j+4}) \leq c({\bf y})$, which proves the lemma. Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{j+2},x_{j+3})$ was found in $B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$. Then $n= L ( x_{j+2},x_{j+3} )$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the lemma to $c(x_{j+1},x_{j+4}) \le c({\bf y})$ and name the level $n$.

nodes.name: Case $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) < n$
nodes.statement: So first suppose $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) < n$. Then $x$ was found in the complement of \[ B(x_j,2\lambda^n) \cup B(x_{j+1},2\lambda^n). \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower flanking level: the centre was chosen outside the relevant balls.

nodes.name: Case $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) = n$
nodes.statement: If instead $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) = n$, then let $y \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_j,x_{j+1})$ was found in $B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$. We may assume that $x\neq y$, otherwise $\{x_j,x_{j+1}\}=\{x_{j+2},x_{j+3}\}$ and the claim is obvious. Hence, we have that $\rho(x,y) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and so \[ B_\rho(x,\lambda^n) \cap B_\rho(y,\lambda^n) = \emptyset. \] As $x_{j+1} \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$, we get that $x_{j+1} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$. A similar argument holds for $x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal level: distinct net points are $4\lambda^n$-apart so the balls are disjoint.

nodes.name: Apply the shortcut inequality
nodes.statement: Thus, we have that the claim follows from \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption2} if we set $x_i=x$, $q_{i,1} = x_{j+2}$, $q_{i,2} = x_{j+3}$, $p_1 = x_{j+1}$, and $p_2 = x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the metric assumption with the four points to conclude.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (reduction to $\I^*$ with multiplicity at most 4)
nodes.statement: For any $\x \in \I_A$, there exists $\x' \in \I^*$ such that $\Ext(\x) = \Ext(\x')$, $c(\x') \leq c(\x)$, and \begin{equation} \# L_{\x'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \N. \end{equation} Moreover, $\x$ and $\x'$ have the same first and last shortcuts.
nodes.statement_short: Every alternating itinerary can be replaced by one in $\I^*$ of no greater cost using each level at most 4 times, keeping the first and last shortcuts.
assumptions: For any $\x \in \I_A$
conclusions: there exists $\x' \in \I^*$ such that $\Ext(\x) = \Ext(\x')$, $c(\x') \leq c(\x)$
\# L_{\x'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \N
Moreover, $\x$ and $\x'$ have the same first and last shortcuts.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: Given an initial $\x \in \I_A$, we iterate Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} until we get an itinerary $\x'$ for which there are no indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. As the length of the itinerary shrinks by 2 with each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, we get that we have to stop after some finite number of iterations. It is elementary to see that if $L_{\bf x'} : \{0,\dots,n\} \to \N$ satisfies $$L_{\x'}(i+1) < \max (L_{\x'}(i),L_{\x'}(i+2)), \qquad \forall i \in \{0,\dots,n-2\},$$ then $L_{\x'}$ is decreasing-increasing, which means that $\x' \in \I^*$. Now suppose $\# L_{\x'}^{-1}(k) > 4$ for some $k \in \N$. As $\x' \in \I^*$, we get that there exists some $i \in 2\N$ so that $$L(x_i,x_{i+1}) = L(x_{i+2},x_{i+3}) = L(x_{i+4},x_{i+5}).$$ But this contradicts the assumption that $\x'$ does not have any indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. Finally, since each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} keeps the first and last shortcut of $\x$ unchanged the resulting itinerary $\x'$ has the same first and last shortcut as $\x$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Lemma 3.2 until no reducible index remains; the terminal itinerary is decreasing-increasing and cannot repeat a level more than four times.

nodes.name: Iterate Lemma 3.2 to termination
nodes.statement: Given an initial $\x \in \I_A$, we iterate Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} until we get an itinerary $\x'$ for which there are no indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. As the length of the itinerary shrinks by 2 with each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, we get that we have to stop after some finite number of iterations. It is elementary to see that if $L_{\bf x'} : \{0,\dots,n\} \to \N$ satisfies $$L_{\x'}(i+1) < \max (L_{\x'}(i),L_{\x'}(i+2)), \qquad \forall i \in \{0,\dots,n-2\},$$ then $L_{\x'}$ is decreasing-increasing, which means that $\x' \in \I^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Each application shortens by two, so the process stops and yields an element of $\I^*$.

nodes.name: Multiplicity bound by contradiction
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\# L_{\x'}^{-1}(k) > 4$ for some $k \in \N$. As $\x' \in \I^*$, we get that there exists some $i \in 2\N$ so that $$L(x_i,x_{i+1}) = L(x_{i+2},x_{i+3}) = L(x_{i+4},x_{i+5}).$$ But this contradicts the assumption that $\x'$ does not have any indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}.
nodes.statement_short: Five occurrences of one level would give a reducible index, contradicting termination.

nodes.name: First and last shortcuts are preserved
nodes.statement: Finally, since each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} keeps the first and last shortcut of $\x$ unchanged the resulting itinerary $\x'$ has the same first and last shortcut as $\x$.
nodes.statement_short: Each reduction leaves the extreme shortcuts untouched.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.4 ($d$ is a distance on $X$)
nodes.statement: The function $d$ is a distance on $X$.
conclusions: The function $d$ is a distance on $X$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: The validity of the triangle inequality follows from the definition of the distance as defined in \eqref{eq:ddef}. Symmetry is due to the symmetry of the cost function. What needs to be checked is that $x \ne y$ implies $d(x,y)>0$. In order to show this, suppose that $x,y \in X$ with $\rho(x,y)>0$. Let $n \in \N$ be such that \[ 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \le \frac12\rho(x,y). \] Let $(\alpha_n)$ be the sequence of positive numbers used to construct the cost function in Section~\ref{sec:construction}. Consider the positive number \[ \varepsilon := \min\left(\frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1}, \frac14\rho(x,y)\right). \] Let $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, $c(\x) \leq d(x,y) + \varepsilon$, and $\# L_{\x}^{-1}(k) \leq 4$ for all $k \in \N$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} (remember that using stationary walks every itinerary can be modified to be an alternating itinerary of no greater cost, because of triangle inequality). On the one hand, if $L_\x^{-1}([1,n-1]) = \emptyset$, then the alternating itinerary does not have shortcuts at odd steps and it has them at even steps only of level greater that $n$ and with multiplicity at most $4$. Hence, we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(x,y) & \ge & c(\x) - \varepsilon \ge \sum_{j \text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \varepsilon \ge \rho(x,y) - \sum_{j \text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \frac14\rho(x,y)\\ & \ge & \frac34\rho(x,y) - 4 \sum_{k=n}^\infty 2\lambda^k \ge \frac34\rho(x,y) - 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \ge \frac14\rho(x,y) > 0, \end{eqnarray*} where we used that a point in a shortcuts at level $k$ has $\rho$-distance less than $ \lambda^k$ from the center of the ball in which the shortcut was found. On the other hand, if $L_\x^{-1}([1,n-1]) \ne \emptyset$, then, if $(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell)$ is a shortcut at level $l<n$ of $\x$, we have \[ d(x,y) \ge c(\x) - \varepsilon \ge c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) - \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} \ge \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} > 0, \] where we used that $ c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) = \alpha_l \rho(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) \geq \alpha_l \lambda^l.$ In both cases $d(x,y) > 0$ as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Only positivity needs work: choose a near-optimal itinerary in $\I^*$ and split on whether it uses a shortcut of level below $n$.

nodes.name: Reduce to positivity and set up $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: The validity of the triangle inequality follows from the definition of the distance as defined in \eqref{eq:ddef}. Symmetry is due to the symmetry of the cost function. What needs to be checked is that $x \ne y$ implies $d(x,y)>0$. In order to show this, suppose that $x,y \in X$ with $\rho(x,y)>0$. Let $n \in \N$ be such that \[ 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \le \frac12\rho(x,y). \] Let $(\alpha_n)$ be the sequence of positive numbers used to construct the cost function in Section~\ref{sec:construction}. Consider the positive number \[ \varepsilon := \min\left(\frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1}, \frac14\rho(x,y)\right). \] Let $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, $c(\x) \leq d(x,y) + \varepsilon$, and $\# L_{\x}^{-1}(k) \leq 4$ for all $k \in \N$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} (remember that using stationary walks every itinerary can be modified to be an alternating itinerary of no greater cost, because of triangle inequality).
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry and triangle inequality are free; fix $n$, $\varepsilon$ and a near-optimal $\x \in \I^*$.

nodes.name: Case: no shortcut of level below $n$
nodes.statement: On the one hand, if $L_\x^{-1}([1,n-1]) = \emptyset$, then the alternating itinerary does not have shortcuts at odd steps and it has them at even steps only of level greater that $n$ and with multiplicity at most $4$. Hence, we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(x,y) & \ge & c(\x) - \varepsilon \ge \sum_{j \text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \varepsilon \ge \rho(x,y) - \sum_{j \text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \frac14\rho(x,y)\\ & \ge & \frac34\rho(x,y) - 4 \sum_{k=n}^\infty 2\lambda^k \ge \frac34\rho(x,y) - 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \ge \frac14\rho(x,y) > 0, \end{eqnarray*} where we used that a point in a shortcuts at level $k$ has $\rho$-distance less than $ \lambda^k$ from the center of the ball in which the shortcut was found.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the odd (walking) steps and subtract the geometric tail of high-level flights.

nodes.name: Case: a shortcut of level below $n$ occurs
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $L_\x^{-1}([1,n-1]) \ne \emptyset$, then, if $(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell)$ is a shortcut at level $l<n$ of $\x$, we have \[ d(x,y) \ge c(\x) - \varepsilon \ge c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) - \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} \ge \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} > 0, \] where we used that $ c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) = \alpha_l \rho(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) \geq \alpha_l \lambda^l.$ In both cases $d(x,y) > 0$ as needed.
nodes.statement_short: A single low-level flight already costs at least $\frac12\min_k \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} > 0$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.5 (at most one low-level shortcut meets a small ball)
nodes.statement: Let $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \lambda^n$. There exists at most one pair $\{q_1,q_2\}$ such that $(q_1,q_2) \in \S$, $L(q_1,q_2) < n$ and $\{q_1,q_2\} \cap B_d(x,r) \ne \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: A $d$-ball of radius $r < \lambda^n$ meets the endpoints of at most one shortcut of level below $n$.
assumptions: Let $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \lambda^n$.
conclusions: There exists at most one pair $\{q_1,q_2\}$ such that $(q_1,q_2) \in \S$, $L(q_1,q_2) < n$ and $\{q_1,q_2\} \cap B_d(x,r) \ne \emptyset$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: Suppose to the contrary that there exist two disjoint $(q_1,q_2), (\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) \in \S$ with \begin{equation} L(q_1,q_2), L(\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) < n \end{equation} and $q_1,\tilde q_1 \in B_d(x,r)$. Then \[ d(q_1,\tilde q_1) \le d(q_1,x) + d(x,\tilde q_1) < 2r \le 2\lambda^n. \] Let $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $x_0=q_1,$ $x_N=\tilde q_1$ and \begin{equation} c(\x) < 2\lambda^n. \end{equation} We may assume that $N$ is odd, up to adding a stationary walk at the end. Hence the slightly longer itinerary ${\bf y}=(q_2,q_2,q_1,x_1,\dots,x_{N-1}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2)$ is an alternating itinerary. By applying Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} to ${\bf y}$ we know that there exists $ {\bf y}' \in \I^*$ such that $ c( {\bf y}') \le c( {\bf y}), $ where $ {\rm Ext}( {\bf y}') ={\rm Ext} ( {\bf y}) $. Notice that, since the construction in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} keeps the the first and last shortcuts stay the same, we have that ${\bf y}'$ is of the form \[{\bf y}' = (q_2,q_2,q_1,x'_1,\dots,x'_{N'}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) .\] We conclude that the itinerary $\x$ may be replaced with no extra cost by an itinerary $\x'$ that is decreasing-increasing and, due to \eqref{e:shortcut-lower-bnds}, we have $L_\x^{-1}([n,\infty]) = \emptyset$. We remark that the itinerary $\x'$ cannot have only stationary walks, i.e., there is some $j \in 2\Z$ so that $x'_j \neq x'_{j+1}$. Indeed, otherwise the itinerary cannot move away from $\{q_1,q_2\}$, since distinct shortcuts are separated. Hence, there are two distinct shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Set $k_1:= L(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$ $k_2:= L(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Recall that $k_1,k_2<n$. Let $a, b$ are the centers of the balls in which the shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$ were found with radii $\lambda^{k_1}$ and $\lambda^{k_2}$, respectively. Let us distinguish two cases. Assume first that $k_1=k_2=:k$, so that $a$ and $ b$ are $4\lambda^{k}$ separated. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(a,b) -\rho(a,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k} - \lambda^{k}- \lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^n. \] Suppose now $k_1\neq k_2$, say that $k_1< k_2$, the other case is similar. Recall that $b$ was found outside $B(x'_j,4\lambda^{k_2})$ in the construction of the shortcuts. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(b,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k_2} - \lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^n. \] In either case we have \[ c(\x) \ge c(\x') \ge \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge 2\lambda^n, \] which is in contradiction with \eqref{eq:q1q1small}.
nodes.statement_short: Assume two such shortcuts, build an alternating itinerary through both, and derive a $\ge 2\lambda^n$ walking cost contradicting the assumed small cost.

nodes.name: Set up the contradiction and the enlarged itinerary
nodes.statement: Suppose to the contrary that there exist two disjoint $(q_1,q_2), (\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) \in \S$ with \begin{equation} L(q_1,q_2), L(\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) < n \end{equation} and $q_1,\tilde q_1 \in B_d(x,r)$. Then \[ d(q_1,\tilde q_1) \le d(q_1,x) + d(x,\tilde q_1) < 2r \le 2\lambda^n. \] Let $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $x_0=q_1,$ $x_N=\tilde q_1$ and \begin{equation} c(\x) < 2\lambda^n. \end{equation} We may assume that $N$ is odd, up to adding a stationary walk at the end. Hence the slightly longer itinerary ${\bf y}=(q_2,q_2,q_1,x_1,\dots,x_{N-1}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2)$ is an alternating itinerary. By applying Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} to ${\bf y}$ we know that there exists $ {\bf y}' \in \I^*$ such that $ c( {\bf y}') \le c( {\bf y}), $ where $ {\rm Ext}( {\bf y}') ={\rm Ext} ( {\bf y}) $. Notice that, since the construction in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} keeps the the first and last shortcuts stay the same, we have that ${\bf y}'$ is of the form \[{\bf y}' = (q_2,q_2,q_1,x'_1,\dots,x'_{N'}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) .\] We conclude that the itinerary $\x$ may be replaced with no extra cost by an itinerary $\x'$ that is decreasing-increasing and, due to \eqref{e:shortcut-lower-bnds}, we have $L_\x^{-1}([n,\infty]) = \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose two low-level shortcuts meet the ball; pad the connecting itinerary to be alternating and reduce it via Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: Locate two distinct shortcuts in the reduced itinerary
nodes.statement: We remark that the itinerary $\x'$ cannot have only stationary walks, i.e., there is some $j \in 2\Z$ so that $x'_j \neq x'_{j+1}$. Indeed, otherwise the itinerary cannot move away from $\{q_1,q_2\}$, since distinct shortcuts are separated. Hence, there are two distinct shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Set $k_1:= L(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$ $k_2:= L(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Recall that $k_1,k_2<n$. Let $a, b$ are the centers of the balls in which the shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$ were found with radii $\lambda^{k_1}$ and $\lambda^{k_2}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: The itinerary must actually move, so it contains two distinct shortcuts with centres $a,b$.

nodes.name: Case $k_1 = k_2$
nodes.statement: Assume first that $k_1=k_2=:k$, so that $a$ and $ b$ are $4\lambda^{k}$ separated. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(a,b) -\rho(a,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k} - \lambda^{k}- \lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equal levels: the centres are $4\lambda^k$-separated.

nodes.name: Case $k_1 \ne k_2$ and conclusion
nodes.statement: Suppose now $k_1\neq k_2$, say that $k_1< k_2$, the other case is similar. Recall that $b$ was found outside $B(x'_j,4\lambda^{k_2})$ in the construction of the shortcuts. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(b,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k_2} - \lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^n. \] In either case we have \[ c(\x) \ge c(\x') \ge \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge 2\lambda^n, \] which is in contradiction with \eqref{eq:q1q1small}.
nodes.statement_short: Unequal levels give an even larger gap; either way the walking cost exceeds $2\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.6 (comparison of $\rho$-balls and $d$-balls)
nodes.statement: For all $x \in X$ and $r > 0$ there exist $y_1,y_2 \in X$ such that \begin{equation} B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r) \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Every $d$-ball is squeezed between a $\rho$-ball of the same radius and a $\rho$-ball around at most two centres with a controlled radius blow-up.
assumptions: For all $x \in X$ and $r > 0$
conclusions: there exist $y_1,y_2 \in X$ such that \begin{equation} B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r) \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: The first inclusion $B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)$ follows from the fact that by construction $d \le \rho$. Let us show the second inclusion. Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $\Ext(\x)=(x,z)$, $c(\x) \leq r$, and $\# L_\x^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \N$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$. Now suppose that $r < 1$ and let $n \in \N \cup\{0\}$ be such that \[ \lambda^{n+1} \le r < \lambda^n. \] By Lemma~\ref{lma:largegaps} there exists at most one pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ such that $(y_1,y_2) \in \S$ and \begin{equation} L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset. \end{equation} If such pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ does not exist, we define $y_1 = y_2 = x$. Now \[ B_d(x,r) \subset B_d(\{y_1,y_2\},2r). \] Take $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By symmetry we may suppose $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(y_1,z)$, $c({\bf x}) < 2r$, and $\# L_\x^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \N$. By the assumption $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$ we may assume that ${\bf x}$ does not contain the shortcuts $(y_1,y_2),(y_2,y_1)$. Then by \eqref{eq:onlyonebigjump} we have $L(x_{j-1},x_j) \ge n$ for all $j$ even. Then, by the fact that ${\bf x} \in \I^*$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(y_1,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = n}^\infty \lambda^k = 2r + 8\frac{\lambda^n}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $ \lambda^{n+1} \le r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds.
nodes.statement_short: The first inclusion is $d \le \rho$; for the second, bound the $\rho$-length of a near-optimal $\I^*$ itinerary, splitting on $r \ge 1$ and $r < 1$.

nodes.name: First inclusion
nodes.statement: The first inclusion $B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)$ follows from the fact that by construction $d \le \rho$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from $d \le \rho$.

nodes.name: Case $r \ge 1$
nodes.statement: Let us show the second inclusion. Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $\Ext(\x)=(x,z)$, $c(\x) \leq r$, and $\# L_\x^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \N$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$.
nodes.statement_short: Large radii: the flight tail $8\sum\lambda^k$ is absorbed into $r$.

nodes.name: Case $r < 1$
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $r < 1$ and let $n \in \N \cup\{0\}$ be such that \[ \lambda^{n+1} \le r < \lambda^n. \] By Lemma~\ref{lma:largegaps} there exists at most one pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ such that $(y_1,y_2) \in \S$ and \begin{equation} L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset. \end{equation} If such pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ does not exist, we define $y_1 = y_2 = x$. Now \[ B_d(x,r) \subset B_d(\{y_1,y_2\},2r). \] Take $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By symmetry we may suppose $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(y_1,z)$, $c({\bf x}) < 2r$, and $\# L_\x^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \N$. By the assumption $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$ we may assume that ${\bf x}$ does not contain the shortcuts $(y_1,y_2),(y_2,y_1)$. Then by \eqref{eq:onlyonebigjump} we have $L(x_{j-1},x_j) \ge n$ for all $j$ even. Then, by the fact that ${\bf x} \in \I^*$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(y_1,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = n}^\infty \lambda^k = 2r + 8\frac{\lambda^n}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $ \lambda^{n+1} \le r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Small radii: use Lemma 3.5 to find the at most one low-level shortcut pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ and bound the tail from level $n$.

nodes.name: Proof that $(X,d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular
nodes.statement: We now give the proof of the Ahlfors $Q$-regularity of the space $(X,d)$, assuming that $(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular. Namely, we have that there exists a constant $C < \infty$ such that \[ \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_\rho(x,r)) \le Cr^Q, \] for all $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \diam_\rho(X)$. Hence by Lemma~\ref{lma:inclusions} we have \[ \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_d(x,r)) \le C2(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2))^Qr^Q, \] for all $x \in X$ and $0 < (2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2))r < \diam_\rho(X)$. Thus $(X,d)$ is also Ahlfors $Q$-regular.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $\mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_d(x,r))$ using the ball inclusions of Lemma 3.6 and the Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$.

nodes.name: Proof that $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on any set of positive measure
nodes.statement: Let $A\subseteq X$ be such that $\H^4_{\rho}(A)>0$. Our aim is to show that $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. For this purpose take a density-point $x$ of $A$. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $r_\epsilon > 0$ such that \[ B_\rho(x,r) \subset B_\rho(A,\epsilon r), \qquad \text{for all }r \in (0,r_\epsilon). \] Now, for all $n \in \N$ there exists $(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) \in \S$ with $L(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) = n$ such that \[ \{q_{n,1},q_{n,2}\} \subset B_\rho(x,2c_E\lambda^n). \] If $3c_E\lambda^n < r_\epsilon$, there exist $x_{n,1},x_{n,2} \in A$ such that \[ \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \qquad \text{and}\qquad \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n. \] Then \[ \rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) \ge \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) - \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) - \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \] and \begin{eqnarray*} d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) & \le & d(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + d(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + d(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & \alpha_n \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & 2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore we have \[ \frac{d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})}{\rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})} \le \frac{2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n}{\lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n} = \frac{2\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon}{\lambda-6c_E\epsilon}. \] As $\alpha_n \to 0$, by letting $n$ be sufficiently large and $\epsilon$ be sufficiently small, we get that $\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon$ is sufficently small and so the distances $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.statement_short: At a density point of $A$, pick points of $A$ near the level $n$ shortcut endpoints; the ratio $d/\rho$ there is $O(\alpha_n + \epsilon)$, which tends to $0$.

nodes.name: Take a density point and nearby shortcut endpoints
nodes.statement: For this purpose take a density-point $x$ of $A$. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $r_\epsilon > 0$ such that \[ B_\rho(x,r) \subset B_\rho(A,\epsilon r), \qquad \text{for all }r \in (0,r_\epsilon). \] Now, for all $n \in \N$ there exists $(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) \in \S$ with $L(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) = n$ such that \[ \{q_{n,1},q_{n,2}\} \subset B_\rho(x,2c_E\lambda^n). \] If $3c_E\lambda^n < r_\epsilon$, there exist $x_{n,1},x_{n,2} \in A$ such that \[ \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \qquad \text{and}\qquad \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: At a density point, find points of $A$ within $3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n$ of each level $n$ shortcut endpoint.

nodes.name: Bound $\rho$ from below and $d$ from above
nodes.statement: Then \[ \rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) \ge \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) - \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) - \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \] and \begin{eqnarray*} d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) & \le & d(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + d(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + d(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & \alpha_n \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & 2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequalities give $\rho \ge \lambda^{n+1}-6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n$ and $d \le 2\alpha_n\lambda^n+6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Let $\alpha_n \to 0$
nodes.statement: Therefore we have \[ \frac{d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})}{\rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})} \le \frac{2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n}{\lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n} = \frac{2\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon}{\lambda-6c_E\epsilon}. \] As $\alpha_n \to 0$, by letting $n$ be sufficiently large and $\epsilon$ be sufficiently small, we get that $\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon$ is sufficently small and so the distances $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.statement_short: The ratio $(2\alpha_n+6c_E\epsilon)/(\lambda-6c_E\epsilon)$ can be made arbitrarily small.

nodes.name: Remark 3.7 (zero costs are allowed)
nodes.statement: In the definition of the costs for the shortcuts we could also allow $\alpha_n = 0$. This would give a semi-distance on $X$ that, upon factoring, gives a metric space $(Y,d)$ that satisfies all the previous properties.
nodes.statement_short: Allowing $\alpha_n = 0$ yields a semi-distance whose quotient metric space still has all the stated properties.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: We will verify that the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold in the Heisenberg group with $\lambda = \frac12$. Let $p \in \mathbb H$ and $r > 0$. By left-translation invariance of the distance $d_b$ in $\mathbb H$ we may assume that $p = (0,0,0)$. Take $q_1 = (0,0,0)$ and $q_2 = (0,0,r^2/4)$. Now let $p_1,p_2 \notin B(0,r)$. Since $d_b(q_1,q_2) = \sqrt{r^2/4} = r/2$, by the triangle inequality we have that $d_b(p_1,q_1) \ge r/2$ and $d_b(p_2,q_2) \ge r/2$. Write $p_1 = (x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $p_2 = (x_2,y_2,z_2)$. Then the equation for the box distance is given by \eqref{eq:box:dist}. Trivially, we have \[ |x_1-x_2| \le |x_1| + |x_2| \le d_b(p_1,q_1) + d_b(p_2,q_2) \] and \[ |y_2-y_1| \le |y_1| + |y_2| \le d_b(p_1,q_1) + d_b(p_2,q_2). \] By using the triangle inequality and the estimate $r^2/4 \le d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)$ we also get \begin{eqnarray*} \left|z_1-z_2-\frac12(x_1y_2-x_2y_1) \right| & \le & |z_1|+|z_2-\frac14r^2|+\frac14r^2 +\frac12|x_1||y_2| + \frac12|x_2||y_1|\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2+d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & & +\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+2d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2\\ & = & \left(d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2)\right)^2. \end{eqnarray*} Thus we have \[ d_b(p_1,p_2) \le d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2) \] as required by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the hypotheses of Theorem 1.3 in $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ with $\lambda = \frac12$, using the vertical pair $q_1=0$, $q_2=(0,0,r^2/4)$.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1 (snowflakes of Ahlfors regular spaces admit shortcuts)
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be an Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space with $Q > 0$ and let $\delta \in (0,1)$. Then the snowflaked metric space $(X,d^\delta)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}. Consequently, there exists a distance $d'$ on $X$ such that $d' \le d^\delta$, $(X,d')$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular, and for any $A\subseteq X$ with $\H^{Q/\delta}_{d^\delta}(A)>0$, we have that $d'$ and $d^\delta$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Shortcuts in snowflaked Ahlfors regular metric spaces
nodes.statement_short: Any snowflake $(X,d^\delta)$ of an Ahlfors $Q$-regular space satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 1.3, so it carries a shortened Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular distance with no biLipschitz pieces.
assumptions: Let $(X,d)$ be an Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space with $Q > 0$ and let $\delta \in (0,1)$.
conclusions: Then the snowflaked metric space $(X,d^\delta)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}.

Consequently, there exists a distance $d'$ on $X$ such that $d' \le d^\delta$, $(X,d')$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular, and for any $A\subseteq X$ with $\H^{Q/\delta}_{d^\delta}(A)>0$, we have that $d'$ and $d^\delta$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: First of all, it is trivial that $(X,d^\delta)$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular. Let us then check the assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}. Since $(X,d)$ is $Q$-regular, there exists $C > 1$ such that \begin{equation} \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q(B_d(x,r)) \le Cr^Q \end{equation} for all $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \diam(X)$. We shall set $\lambda:= (2C)^{-2\delta/Q}(1-\delta)^\delta$. Take $p \in X$ and $0 < r < \diam(X)$. Define $q_1 = p$ and take \[ q_2 \in B_d(p,(1-\delta)r^\frac{1}{\delta}) \setminus B_d(p, (2C)^{-2/Q}(1-\delta) r^\frac{1}{\delta}). \] Such $q_2$ exists since the annulus from where the point is taken has positive measure by \eqref{eq:ahlfors} and is hence non-empty. In particular, $q_1, q_2\in B_{d^\delta} (p,r)$ and \[ d(q_1,q_2)^\delta \ge \left((2C)^{-2/Q}(1-\delta)\right)^\delta r = \lambda r. \] Now, take $p_1,p_2 \notin B_d\left(p,r^\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$. We get that $$ d(q_1,p_1),d(q_2,p_2) \geq \delta r^{1/\delta},$$ and so $$d(q_1,q_2) \leq \left( 1 - \delta\right) r^{1/\delta} \leq \left( \frac{1}{\delta} - 1 \right) \min(d(q_1,p_1),d(q_2,p_2)).$$ First assume that $d(p_1,q_1) \le d(p_2,q_2)$. Then we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(p_1,p_2)^\delta & \le & (d(p_1,q_1)+d(q_1,q_2)+d(p_2,q_2))^\delta \\ & \le & ((1+(\frac1\delta-1))d(p_1,q_1)+d(p_2,q_2))^\delta\\ & \le & d(p_2,q_2)^\delta + \delta(1+(\frac1\delta-1))d(p_1,q_1)d(p_2,q_2)^{1-\delta} \\ & \le & d(p_1,q_1)^\delta + d(p_2,q_2)^\delta \end{eqnarray*} verifying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption}. In the penultimate inequality, we used the fact that $x \mapsto x^\delta$ is concave so that the higher order terms of the Taylor expansion is always negative. An analogous calculation takes care of the case $d(p_2,q_2) \leq d(p_1,q_1)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Shortcuts in snowflaked Ahlfors regular metric spaces
nodes.statement_short: Choose $q_2$ in an annulus of positive measure around $p$, then use concavity of $x \mapsto x^\delta$ to verify the shortcut inequality.

nodes.name: self-similar tiling similitudes $S_{i,j,k}$ and the attractor $K$
nodes.statement: Define the similitude mappings as \[ S_{i,j,k}(p) = \left(\frac{i}{2},\frac{j}{2},\frac{k}{4}\right) \cdot \delta_\frac12(p), \qquad i,j \in \{0,1\}, k \in \{0,1,2,3\}. \] Relabel the similitudes by $\{S_i\,:\,i = 1,\dots,16\} = \{S_{i,j,k}\}$ and denote by $K$ the attractor of $\{S_{i,j,k}\}$, i.e., the nonempty compact set (see \cite{Hutchinson} for details) satisfying \begin{equation} K = \bigcup_{i=1}^{16}S_i(K). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sixteen half-scale similitudes of $\mathbb H$ whose attractor is the compact set $K$.

nodes.name: $K$ has nonempty interior and $(K,d_b)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular
nodes.statement: Because of the nonempty interior and the self-similar structure $(K,d_b)$ is Ahlfors $4$-regular.
assumptions: Because of the nonempty interior and the self-similar structure
conclusions: $(K,d_b)$ is Ahlfors $4$-regular

nodes.name: Proof that $K$ has nonempty interior
nodes.statement: Let us show that $K$ has nonempty interior. First of all, the horizontal projection of the iterated function system has the unit square as the attractor. Secondly, since the dilation and the group operation commute, we may consider separately the horizontal and vertical components of the iterated function system. This way we see that \begin{equation} K = \{(x,y,z+t) \,:\, (x,y,z) \in \widetilde K, t \in [0,1]\}, \end{equation} where $\widetilde K$ is the attractor of the horizontal component that is realized as the attractor of the system \[ \{S_{i,j,0}\,:\, i,j \in \{0,1\}\}. \] The set $\widetilde K$ has the form \begin{equation} \widetilde K = \overline{\{(x,y,\varphi(x,y))\,:\,(x,y)\in [0,1]^2\}} \end{equation} with some Borel function $\varphi \colon [0,1]^2 \to \R$. Observe that $\varphi$ is bounded since $K$ is compact. Also, since $0$ is the fixed point of $S_{0,0,0}$ and $S_{i,j,0}(\widetilde K)$ do not contain $0$ if $i\ne 0$ or $j \ne 0$, the function $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$. Therefore by \eqref{eq:Kformula} the attractor $K$ contains a small ball near $0$ and thus $K$ has nonempty interior.
nodes.statement_short: Split the IFS into horizontal and vertical parts; the horizontal attractor is a graph over the unit square whose defining function is continuous at $0$, so $K$ contains a ball near $0$.

nodes.name: Horizontal projection is the unit square
nodes.statement: First of all, the horizontal projection of the iterated function system has the unit square as the attractor.
nodes.statement_short: The projected IFS has the unit square as attractor.

nodes.name: Split horizontal and vertical components
nodes.statement: Secondly, since the dilation and the group operation commute, we may consider separately the horizontal and vertical components of the iterated function system. This way we see that \begin{equation} K = \{(x,y,z+t) \,:\, (x,y,z) \in \widetilde K, t \in [0,1]\}, \end{equation} where $\widetilde K$ is the attractor of the horizontal component that is realized as the attractor of the system \[ \{S_{i,j,0}\,:\, i,j \in \{0,1\}\}. \] The set $\widetilde K$ has the form \begin{equation} \widetilde K = \overline{\{(x,y,\varphi(x,y))\,:\,(x,y)\in [0,1]^2\}} \end{equation} with some Borel function $\varphi \colon [0,1]^2 \to \R$.
nodes.statement_short: Dilation commutes with the group law, so $K$ is a vertical $[0,1]$-thickening of a graph $\widetilde K$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $\varphi$ at $0$
nodes.statement: Observe that $\varphi$ is bounded since $K$ is compact. Also, since $0$ is the fixed point of $S_{0,0,0}$ and $S_{i,j,0}(\widetilde K)$ do not contain $0$ if $i\ne 0$ or $j \ne 0$, the function $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$. Therefore by \eqref{eq:Kformula} the attractor $K$ contains a small ball near $0$ and thus $K$ has nonempty interior.
