nodes.name: Self-similar construction of the shortcuts on $K$
nodes.statement: We define the shortcuts at level $n$ as \[ \S_n := \{(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,\frac1{64}))\,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\}. \] We also set $L(x,y) = n$ for $(x,y) \in \S_n$. Note that levels start from $n = 3$. We then define the total set of shortcuts as \[ \S := \bigcup_{n=3}^\infty \S_n. \] Define the cost as $c(x,y) = 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \S$.
nodes.statement_short: Place one vertical shortcut pair at the image of $(\frac12,\frac12,0)$ under each level $n-3$ word of similitudes, with level $n$ and zero cost.
output: Define the cost as $c(x,y) = 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \S$.

nodes.name: Level $n$ shortcuts
nodes.statement: We define the shortcuts at level $n$ as \[ \S_n := \{(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,\frac1{64}))\,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take the vertical pair $(\frac12,\frac12,0),(\frac12,\frac12,\frac1{64})$ pushed forward by each word of length $n-3$.

nodes.name: Assign levels and take the union
nodes.statement: We also set $L(x,y) = n$ for $(x,y) \in \S_n$. Note that levels start from $n = 3$. We then define the total set of shortcuts as \[ \S := \bigcup_{n=3}^\infty \S_n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Levels start at $n=3$; union over all levels gives $\S$.

nodes.name: Set zero costs
nodes.statement: Define the cost as $c(x,y) = 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \S$.
nodes.statement_short: All shortcuts are free.

nodes.name: horizontal projection $\pi$
nodes.statement: In the following lemmas we will use the map \[\pi : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to \R^2\] that is the projection onto the $xy$-plane and is a $1$-Lipschitz homomorphism, when we endow $\R^2$ with the $\ell_\infty$-distance.
differentia: is a $1$-Lipschitz homomorphism, when we endow $\R^2$ with the $\ell_\infty$-distance

nodes.name: Lemma 5.1 (level $n$ shortcut points avoid neighborhoods of lower levels)
nodes.statement: For all $n \geq 3$, we have \[ \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \cap \left( \bigcup_{m < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in \S_m} B_{d_b}(\{x,y\},2^{-n+2}) \right) = \emptyset. \]
nodes.statement_short: Level $n$ shortcut base points lie outside the $2^{-n+2}$-neighborhood of all lower-level shortcut points.
assumptions: For all $n \geq 3$
conclusions: \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \cap \left( \bigcup_{m < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in \S_m} B_{d_b}(\{x,y\},2^{-n+2}) \right) = \emptyset.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Let $A_k \subset [0,1]^2$ be the centers of the dyadic subcubes of level $k$. Note that for each $k$ we have that \[ \pi(\{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,t) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k, t \in \R\}) = A_k. \] As $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that \[ A_n \cap B_{\R^2_\infty} \left( \bigcup_{m < n} A_m, 2^{-n-1} \right) = \emptyset. \] But this follows from the geometry of $(\R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$. Note that we need the sets $B_{\R^2_\infty}$ to be open, which is fine.
nodes.statement_short: Project by the 1-Lipschitz map $\pi$ and use the dyadic-cube-centre geometry of $(\R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$.

nodes.name: Identify the projections with dyadic centres
nodes.statement: Let $A_k \subset [0,1]^2$ be the centers of the dyadic subcubes of level $k$. Note that for each $k$ we have that \[ \pi(\{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,t) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k, t \in \R\}) = A_k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Under $\pi$, the level $k$ base points map onto the dyadic cube centres $A_k$.

nodes.name: Reduce to planar geometry
nodes.statement: As $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that \[ A_n \cap B_{\R^2_\infty} \left( \bigcup_{m < n} A_m, 2^{-n-1} \right) = \emptyset. \] But this follows from the geometry of $(\R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$. Note that we need the sets $B_{\R^2_\infty}$ to be open, which is fine.
nodes.statement_short: 1-Lipschitzness reduces the claim to disjointness of dyadic centre families in the sup-norm plane.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.2 (level $n$ shortcut points are $2^{-n+2}$-separated)
nodes.statement: For all $n \geq 3$ the set \[ A:= \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \] is $2^{-n+2}$-separated (note: $2^{-n+2} = 4 \cdot 2^{-n}$, which is needed for the construction).
assumptions: For all $n \geq 3$
conclusions: is $2^{-n+2}$-separated

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: As shown in the previous lemma, the image of $A$ under $\pi$ is precisely the centers of the dyadic subcubes of $[0,1]$ of level $n-3$. Let $x,y \in A$ and suppose $\pi(x) \neq \pi(y)$. Then \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \|\pi(x) - \pi(y)\| \geq 2^{-n+3}. \] Now suppose $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ but $x \neq y$. Then as the vertical component of the iterated function system can be viewed independently, we see that the $z$-coordinate of $x$ and $y$ are points in the center of the level $n-3$ 4-dic subintervals of $[\varphi(\pi(x)),\varphi(\pi(x))+1]$, where $\varphi$ is the function in \eqref{eq:phidef}. Thus, they differ by no less than $4^{-n+3}$ and so \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \sqrt{4^{-n+3}} = 2^{-n+3}>2^{-n+2} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Split on whether the horizontal projections of two base points agree; if they do, the $z$-coordinates lie in distinct $4$-adic subintervals.

nodes.name: Case of distinct projections
nodes.statement: Let $x,y \in A$ and suppose $\pi(x) \neq \pi(y)$. Then \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \|\pi(x) - \pi(y)\| \geq 2^{-n+3}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Distinct dyadic centres are $2^{-n+3}$ apart, and $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz.

nodes.name: Case of equal projections
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ but $x \neq y$. Then as the vertical component of the iterated function system can be viewed independently, we see that the $z$-coordinate of $x$ and $y$ are points in the center of the level $n-3$ 4-dic subintervals of $[\varphi(\pi(x)),\varphi(\pi(x))+1]$, where $\varphi$ is the function in \eqref{eq:phidef}. Thus, they differ by no less than $4^{-n+3}$ and so \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \sqrt{4^{-n+3}} = 2^{-n+3}>2^{-n+2} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Same projection: the vertical coordinates differ by at least $4^{-n+3}$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.3 (level $n$ shortcut points $c_E2^{-n}$-cover $K$)
nodes.statement: There exists some absolute constant $c_E > 0$ so that \begin{equation} K \subseteq \bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}), \qquad \forall n \geq 3. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For some absolute $c_E$, the level $n$ base points give a $c_E2^{-n}$-covering of $K$ for every $n \ge 3$.
assumptions: There exists some absolute constant $c_E > 0$
conclusions: K \subseteq \bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}), \qquad \forall n \geq 3.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: We prove the claim by induction. As $K$ is bounded, we easily get \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} for $n=3$ by choosing some $c_E$ large enough. Now assume that \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for some $n \ge 3$. Then by the self-similarity of $K$ as exhibited in \eqref{e:K-self-similar} we get \begin{eqnarray*} K& = & \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}))\\ & = &\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-2}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n-1}) \end{eqnarray*} Thus \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$: the base case follows from boundedness of $K$, and the step from the self-similarity $K = \bigcup_i S_i(K)$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove the claim by induction. As $K$ is bounded, we easily get \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} for $n=3$ by choosing some $c_E$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of $K$ gives the case $n=3$ for large $c_E$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now assume that \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for some $n \ge 3$. Then by the self-similarity of $K$ as exhibited in \eqref{e:K-self-similar} we get \begin{eqnarray*} K& = & \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}))\\ & = &\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-2}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n-1}) \end{eqnarray*} Thus \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the 16 similitudes to the covering at level $n$.

nodes.name: The identity map $(K,d_b) \to (K,d)$ is Lipschitz with no biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement: Now the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold for the constructed distance $d$. That is, the identity map $\id \colon (K,d_b) \to (K,d)$ is Lipschitz, but not biLipschitz on any set of positive measure, and the space $(K,d)$ is Ahlfors regular.
assumptions: Now the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold for the constructed distance $d$.
conclusions: the identity map $\id \colon (K,d_b) \to (K,d)$ is Lipschitz, but not biLipschitz on any set of positive measure, and the space $(K,d)$ is Ahlfors regular

nodes.name: What remains to prove Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: In particular, $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ looks down on $(K,d)$. In order to show that $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ is not minimal in looking down, we still need to prove that $(K,d)$ is a BPI space and that $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$.

nodes.name: Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 remain valid in $(K,d)$
nodes.statement: Note that Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} holds in $(K,d)$ as its proof, as well as the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, only require that $\mathcal{N}_{n+1} \cap B_{d_b}(\mathcal{N}_n,4 \lambda^n) = \emptyset$, which holds for the construction of $(K,d)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.4 (small walks between low-level shortcuts)
nodes.statement: Let $\x \in \I^*$ and $n = \min \{k \in \N : L_\x^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}$. There exists $\x' \in \I^*$ such that $\Ext(\x) = \Ext(\x')$, $c(\x') \leq c(\x)$, and for any $j \in \N$ such that $\min (L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}),L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})) = m < n$, then \[ d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \leq 2 \lambda^m. \]
nodes.statement_short: An itinerary in $\I^*$ can be improved so that walks flanked by level $m$ shortcuts have $d_b$-length at most $2\lambda^m$.
assumptions: Let $\x \in \I^*$ and $n = \min \{k \in \N : L_\x^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}$.
conclusions: There exists $\x' \in \I^*$ such that $\Ext(\x) = \Ext(\x')$, $c(\x') \leq c(\x)$
d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \leq 2 \lambda^m.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that there exist $k \in L^{-1}(n)$ such that $k \geq 2j+1$, that is, $L_\x$ is still decreasing from $2j-1$ to $2j+1$. Thus, $L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2}) = m$. Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_m$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})$ is found in $B_{d_b}(x,\lambda^m)$. Then as $L(x_{2j+3},x_{2j+4}) \leq m$, we get that $x_{2j+3} \notin B(x, \lambda^m)$. If $d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) > 2\lambda^m$, then we get that $x_{2j} \notin B(x,\lambda^m)$ by the triangle inequality. Thus, applying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption} with $q_1 = x_{2j+1}$, $q_2 = x_{2j+2}$, $p_1 = x_{2j}$, and $p_2 = x_{2j+3}$, we get that we can replace $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2},x_{2j+3})$ in $\x$ with $(x_{2j},x_{2j+3})$ to get a itinerary in $\I^*$ with lower cost and two fewer points with the same extremal points. We then iterate this procedure until we cannot to get our needed itinerary $\x'$.
nodes.statement_short: If a flanked walk were longer than $2\lambda^m$ the shortcut inequality would let us delete two points, so iterate the replacement.

nodes.name: Replace one long walk
nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that there exist $k \in L^{-1}(n)$ such that $k \geq 2j+1$, that is, $L_\x$ is still decreasing from $2j-1$ to $2j+1$. Thus, $L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2}) = m$. Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_m$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})$ is found in $B_{d_b}(x,\lambda^m)$. Then as $L(x_{2j+3},x_{2j+4}) \leq m$, we get that $x_{2j+3} \notin B(x, \lambda^m)$. If $d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) > 2\lambda^m$, then we get that $x_{2j} \notin B(x,\lambda^m)$ by the triangle inequality. Thus, applying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption} with $q_1 = x_{2j+1}$, $q_2 = x_{2j+2}$, $p_1 = x_{2j}$, and $p_2 = x_{2j+3}$, we get that we can replace $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2},x_{2j+3})$ in $\x$ with $(x_{2j},x_{2j+3})$ to get a itinerary in $\I^*$ with lower cost and two fewer points with the same extremal points.
nodes.statement_short: A walk longer than $2\lambda^m$ puts both flanking points outside $B(x,\lambda^m)$, so the shortcut inequality removes two points.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: We then iterate this procedure until we cannot to get our needed itinerary $\x'$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat until no such walk remains.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.5 (near-optimal itineraries between points of $S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ stay nearby)
nodes.statement: There exists some $C > 0$ so that for all multi-indices ${\mathtt{i}}$, for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in \I^*$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_n\in B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|})$.
nodes.statement_short: Points of $S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ can be joined almost optimally by itineraries staying within $C2^{-|\mathtt{i}|}$ of $S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.
assumptions: for all multi-indices ${\mathtt{i}}$, for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and all $\epsilon > 0$
conclusions: there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in \I^*$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_n\in B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|})$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement:
We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~ef{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary $\x \in \I^*$ such that  egin{enumerate} \item $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, \item $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, \item $\# L_{\x}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad  orall k \in \N$, \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that \[ m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_\x^{-1}(k) 
eq \emptyset\}, \] \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd, \item $L_{\x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$. \end{enumerate} If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in \I^*$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} \] for some $C$ depending on $M$. The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$. Let us prove the claim. Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~ef{lma:K-c1}. Let $M \in \N$ be the minimal even number such that  egin{equation} 2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation} and  egin{equation} 2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation} As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that  egin{equation} d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation} By an application of Lemma~ef{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties. Then \[ c(\x) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] a contradiction. Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied. Now suppose $L_\x^{-1}([0,k-M]) 
eq \emptyset$. Suppose first that $\# L_{\x}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$. Then as $\x \in \I^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) 
otin \S$ such that \[ c(\x) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] which is a contradiction. Then we have by the triangle inequality  egin{multline*} d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \ - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*). \end{multline*} We have that  egin{eqnarray} \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} 
otag \ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray} Together with the fourth property, we get that \[ (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}. \] But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove a six-property claim for words longer than a threshold $M$ by successively applying Lemmas 3.3 and 5.4 and ruling out long walks and low-level shortcuts by cost contradictions.

nodes.name: State the six-property claim
nodes.statement: We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary $\x \in \I^*$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, \item $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, \item $\# L_{\x}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \N$, \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that \[ m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_\x^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}, \] \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd, \item $L_{\x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Claim an itinerary with cost control, bounded multiplicity, short walks and no low-level shortcuts.

nodes.name: Deduce the lemma from the claim
nodes.statement: If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in \I^*$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} \] for some $C$ depending on $M$. The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Summing the short walks gives the $C2^{-|\mathtt{i}|}$ bound; short words are handled by finiteness.

nodes.name: Fix $M$ and get the first four properties
nodes.statement: Let us prove the claim. Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1}. Let $M \in \N$ be the minimal even number such that \begin{equation} 2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation} and \begin{equation} 2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation} As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that \begin{equation} d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation} By an application of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties. We then apply Lemma~\ref{lma:small-walks} on $\x$ (and still calling the result $\x$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $M$ by two explicit inequalities, then apply Lemmas 3.3 and 5.4.

nodes.name: Fifth property: no long walks
nodes.statement: Suppose $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) > 2^{M/2-k}$ for some odd $j$. Then \[ c(\x) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] a contradiction. Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: A walk longer than $2^{M/2-k}$ would cost more than $2d(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Sixth property: no low-level shortcuts
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $L_\x^{-1}([0,k-M]) 
eq \emptyset$. Suppose first that $\# L_{\x}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$. Then as $\x \in \I^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) 
otin \S$ such that \[ c(\x) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] which is a contradiction. Now suppose that $\# L_{\x}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) = 1$. Let $L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) \geq k-M$. Then we have by the triangle inequality  egin{multline*} d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \ - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*). \end{multline*} We have that  egin{eqnarray} \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} 
otag \ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray} Together with the fourth property, we get that \[ (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}. \] But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Two or one low-level shortcuts both contradict $d_b(x,y) \le c_E2^{-2-k}$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.6 (a sub-tile $S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)$ whose optimal itineraries stay inside)
nodes.statement: There exists some multi-index $\mathtt{j}$ such that the following property holds. For any $\epsilon > 0$, $k \in \N$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, and any two $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_N \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: There is a word $\mathtt{j}$ so that points of $S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ are joined near-optimally by itineraries contained in $S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.
assumptions: For any $\epsilon > 0$, $k \in \N$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, and any two $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$
conclusions: there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in \I^*$ with $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_N \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.6
nodes.statement: Let $C > 0$ be the constant from the previous lemma. As $K$ has nonempty interior we may choose $x \in \mathrm{int}(K)$ and $h > 0$ so that $B_{d_b}(x,h) \subset K$. As $K$ is compact, there then exists some $\mathtt{j}$ so that \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq B_{d_b}(x,h) \subseteq K. \] Now let $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ for some arbitrary $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$. Then there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in \I^*$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and each of the points of $\x$ is contained \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|-|\mathtt{j}|}) = S_{\mathtt{i}}(B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|})) \subseteq S_{\mathtt{i}}(K). \]
nodes.statement_short: Use nonempty interior and compactness of $K$ to pick $\mathtt{j}$ with $B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq K$, then push forward by $S_{\mathtt{i}}$.

nodes.name: Choose $\mathtt{j}$ by compactness
nodes.statement: Let $C > 0$ be the constant from the previous lemma. As $K$ has nonempty interior we may choose $x \in \mathrm{int}(K)$ and $h > 0$ so that $B_{d_b}(x,h) \subset K$. As $K$ is compact, there then exists some $\mathtt{j}$ so that \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq B_{d_b}(x,h) \subseteq K. \]
nodes.statement_short: Nonempty interior plus compactness give a word $\mathtt{j}$ whose $C2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}$-neighborhood sits inside $K$.

nodes.name: Push the itinerary forward by $S_{\mathtt{i}}$
nodes.statement: Now let $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ for some arbitrary $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$. Then there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in \I^*$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\Ext(\x) = (x,y)$, and each of the points of $\x$ is contained \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|-|\mathtt{j}|}) = S_{\mathtt{i}}(B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|})) \subseteq S_{\mathtt{i}}(K). \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 5.5 and the similitude scaling to keep the itinerary inside $S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.7 (exact scaling of $d$ on $S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)$)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathtt{j}$ be from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}. Then for all $k \in \N$ and $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, we have that \begin{equation} d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On $S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)$ the similitudes scale the shortcut distance exactly: $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}x,S_{\mathtt{i}}y) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|}d(x,y)$.
assumptions: Let $\mathtt{j}$ be from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}. Then for all $k \in \N$ and $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$
conclusions: d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.7
nodes.statement: If $\x$ is an itinerary from $x$ to $y$, then $S_{\mathtt{i}}(\x)$ is an itinerary from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ with $c(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\x)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} c(\x)$ by the properties of the shortcuts. Thus, we get that $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) \leq 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y)$. For any $\epsilon > 0$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y) \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn} that there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y))$ and $x_j \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$. Thus, applying $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ to $\x$, we get an itinerary $\x'$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $x_j' \in K$ and $c(\x') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c(\x)$. Thus, \[ d(x,y) \leq c(\x') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c(\x) \leq 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)). \] Taking $\epsilon \to 0$ then gives the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Push itineraries forward for `$\le$' and pull the localized near-optimal itineraries of Lemma 5.6 back for `$\ge$'.

nodes.name: Upper bound by pushing forward
nodes.statement: If $\x$ is an itinerary from $x$ to $y$, then $S_{\mathtt{i}}(\x)$ is an itinerary from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ with $c(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\x)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} c(\x)$ by the properties of the shortcuts. Thus, we get that $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) \leq 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Images of itineraries scale costs by $2^{-|\mathtt{i}|}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound by pulling back
nodes.statement: For any $\epsilon > 0$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y) \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn} that there exists an itinerary $\x = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ such that $c(\x) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y))$ and $x_j \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$. Thus, applying $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ to $\x$, we get an itinerary $\x'$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $x_j' \in K$ and $c(\x') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c(\x)$. Thus, \[ d(x,y) \leq c(\x') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c(\x) \leq 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)). \] Taking $\epsilon \to 0$ then gives the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.6 keeps near-optimal itineraries inside $S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, so $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ applies.

nodes.name: Proof that $(K,d)$ is a BPI space
nodes.statement: We can now prove that $K$ is BPI. Let $\mathtt{j}$ be the multi-index from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}, $p_1,p_2 \in K$, and $0 < r_1,r_2 < \diam(K)$. Now there exist two multi-indices $\mathtt{i_1},\mathtt{i_2}$ such that $\diam(S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K)) \ge c r_j$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K) \subset B(p_j,r_j)$ for $j \in \{1,2\}$. Define $A = S_{\mathtt{i_1}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)) \subset B(p_1,r_1)$. Then the map $f \colon A \to B(p_2,r_2)$ defined as $f = S_{\mathtt{i}_2}\circ S_{\mathtt{i}_1}^{-1}$ satisfies \[ d(f(p),f(q)) \overset{\eqref{e:j-invariance}}{=} 2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q \in A. \] Since $\mathcal{H}_d^4(A) \ge c\mathcal{H}_d^4(B(p_1,r_1))$ for some $c$ depending only on $\mathtt{j}$ and $2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}$ is comparable to $r_2/r_1$, we are done with showing that $(K,d)$ is BPI.
nodes.statement_short: Given two balls, choose sub-tiles inside them and use $f = S_{\mathtt{i}_2} \circ S_{\mathtt{i}_1}^{-1}$, which is an exact similarity by Lemma 5.7.

nodes.name: Proof that $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement: By contradiction, suppose that $(K,d)$ does look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$. Then there would exist a closed set $A \subset K$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon (A,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ with $\mathcal{H}^4(f(A))>0$. Since $d \le d_b$, also $f \colon (A,d_b) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ is $L$-Lipschitz. Then $f$ is Pansu-differentiable almost everywhere in $A$. Moreover, the Pansu-differential $Df(x)$ is bijective on a set $A' \subset A$ of positive measure by the area formula: \[ 0 < \mathcal{H}^4(f(A)) \overset{\eqref{e:area-formula}}{\le} \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x). \] Since for all $n,m \in \N$ the set \[ B_{n,m} = K \setminus \bigcup_{k = n}^\infty \bigcup_{ \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k}S_{\mathtt{i}}(K\cap B_{d_b}(0,\frac1m)) \] has $\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}$-measure zero as a porous set, the set \begin{equation} A'' = A' \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty B_{n,m} \end{equation} has positive measure. Let $x \in A''$ be a density point of $A''$. Since $x \in A''$, by the definition \eqref{eq:Adef} there exists a sequence $(n_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ of integers with $n_m \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ and a sequence of multi-indices $\mathtt{i}_m$ with $|\mathtt{i}_m| = n_m$ such that $x \in S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(K)$ for all $m \in \N$ and \[ d_b(x,x_m)< \frac1m 2^{-{n_m}} , \] for all $m \in \N$, where $x_m = S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(0)$. Let $K_m = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(x^{-1}A)\cap K$. Then the functions $f_m \colon (K_m,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ defined as \[ f_m(p) = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))) \] satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p),f_m(q)) & = d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))),\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))) \\ & = 2^{n_m} d_b(f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))) \\ & \le 2^{n_m} L d(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p),x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))\\ & \le L d(S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))\\ & = L d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\\ & \le L \left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\right), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the first inequality follows from the fact that $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and the second inequality from the fact that \[ S_{\mathtt{i}_n}(\S) \subset \S. \] Notice that \begin{equation} d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \le d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \to 0 \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$ since $d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x),0) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. The convergence in \eqref{eq:errorterm} holds uniformly for $p \in K$ by the compactness of $K$. Since $x$ is a density point of $A''$ and hence of $A$, we have that for all $p \in K$ there exists a sequence $(p_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ with $p_m \in K_{n_m}$ and $d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. Along this sequence by the fact that $Df(x)$ is homogeneous we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) & = & d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_{n_m}))),\delta_{2^{{n_m}}}(Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))))\\ &=&2^{n_m} d_b(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m)),Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))) \to 0, \end{eqnarray*} as $m \to \infty$. Hence also \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) & \le d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) + d_b(Df(x)(p_m),Df(x)(p)) \to 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$. Combining the estimates \eqref{eq:fmdestimate}, \eqref{eq:fm_estimate} and \eqref{eq:errorterm} with the fact that $d(p_m,p) \leq d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(Df(x)(p),Df(x)(q)) & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{5.7cm}+ d_b(f_m(p_m),f_m(q_m))\\ & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{0.7cm}+ L\left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p_m,p_m) + d(q_m,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q_m)\right)\\ & &\hspace{3.59cm} + L\left(d(p_m,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,q_m)\right)\\ & \rightarrow & L d(p,q), \qquad \text{as }m \to \infty. \end{eqnarray*} Hence $Df(x)$ is also Lipschitz from $(K,d)$ to $(\mathbb H, d_b)$. Since $Df(x) \colon (\mathbb H, d_b) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is biLipschitz, also the identity map $\id \colon (K, d) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is Lipschitz, but we have shown that this is not the case in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance}.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: A Lipschitz map with positive-measure image would have a bijective Pansu differential at a suitable density point, forcing $\id \colon (K,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ to be Lipschitz, contradicting Theorem 1.2.

nodes.name: Set up the contradiction and apply the area formula
nodes.statement: By contradiction, suppose that $(K,d)$ does look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$. Then there would exist a closed set $A \subset K$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon (A,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ with $\mathcal{H}^4(f(A))>0$. Since $d \le d_b$, also $f \colon (A,d_b) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ is $L$-Lipschitz. Then $f$ is Pansu-differentiable almost everywhere in $A$. Moreover, the Pansu-differential $Df(x)$ is bijective on a set $A' \subset A$ of positive measure by the area formula: \[ 0 < \mathcal{H}^4(f(A)) \overset{\eqref{e:area-formula}}{\le} \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume such a Lipschitz $f$; the area formula makes $Df(x)$ bijective on a positive measure set $A'$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$

nodes.name: Choose a good density point
nodes.statement: Since for all $n,m \in \N$ the set \[ B_{n,m} = K \setminus \bigcup_{k = n}^\infty \bigcup_{ \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k}S_{\mathtt{i}}(K\cap B_{d_b}(0,\frac1m)) \] has $\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}$-measure zero as a porous set, the set \begin{equation} A'' = A' \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty B_{n,m} \end{equation} has positive measure. Let $x \in A''$ be a density point of $A''$. Since $x \in A''$, by the definition \eqref{eq:Adef} there exists a sequence $(n_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ of integers with $n_m \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ and a sequence of multi-indices $\mathtt{i}_m$ with $|\mathtt{i}_m| = n_m$ such that $x \in S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(K)$ for all $m \in \N$ and \[ d_b(x,x_m)< \frac1m 2^{-{n_m}} , \] for all $m \in \N$, where $x_m = S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Remove porous sets to get $A''$, take a density point $x$ and words $\mathtt{i}_m$ with $x$ close to $S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(0)$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$

nodes.name: Rescale $f$ and bound the rescalings
nodes.statement: Let $K_m = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(x^{-1}A)\cap K$. Then the functions $f_m \colon (K_m,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ defined as \[ f_m(p) = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))) \] satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p),f_m(q)) & = d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))),\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))) \\ & = 2^{n_m} d_b(f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))) \\ & \le 2^{n_m} L d(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p),x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))\\ & \le L d(S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))\\ & = L d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\\ & \le L \left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\right), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the first inequality follows from the fact that $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and the second inequality from the fact that \[ S_{\mathtt{i}_n}(\S) \subset \S. \] Notice that \begin{equation} d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \le d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \to 0 \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$ since $d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x),0) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. The convergence in \eqref{eq:errorterm} holds uniformly for $p \in K$ by the compactness of $K$.
nodes.statement_short: The blow-ups $f_m$ obey a Lipschitz-type estimate with an error term tending to $0$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$

nodes.name: Pass to the limit against the Pansu differential
nodes.statement: Since $x$ is a density point of $A''$ and hence of $A$, we have that for all $p \in K$ there exists a sequence $(p_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ with $p_m \in K_{n_m}$ and $d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. Along this sequence by the fact that $Df(x)$ is homogeneous we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) & = & d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_{n_m}))),\delta_{2^{{n_m}}}(Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))))\\ &=&2^{n_m} d_b(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m)),Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))) \to 0, \end{eqnarray*} as $m \to \infty$. Hence also \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) & \le d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) + d_b(Df(x)(p_m),Df(x)(p)) \to 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$. Combining the estimates \eqref{eq:fmdestimate}, \eqref{eq:fm_estimate} and \eqref{eq:errorterm} with the fact that $d(p_m,p) \leq d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(Df(x)(p),Df(x)(q)) & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{5.7cm}+ d_b(f_m(p_m),f_m(q_m))\\ & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{0.7cm}+ L\left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p_m,p_m) + d(q_m,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q_m)\right)\\ & &\hspace{3.59cm} + L\left(d(p_m,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,q_m)\right)\\ & \rightarrow & L d(p,q), \qquad \text{as }m \to \infty. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Along a suitable sequence, $f_m(p_m) \to Df(x)(p)$ and the estimates give $d_b(Df(x)p,Df(x)q) \le Ld(p,q)$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$

nodes.name: Contradiction with Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: Hence $Df(x)$ is also Lipschitz from $(K,d)$ to $(\mathbb H, d_b)$. Since $Df(x) \colon (\mathbb H, d_b) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is biLipschitz, also the identity map $\id \colon (K, d) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is Lipschitz, but we have shown that this is not the case in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance}.
nodes.statement_short: Bijectivity of $Df(x)$ would make the identity $(K,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ Lipschitz.

nodes.name: Local $L$-biLipschitz left-invariance from the Baire Category Theorem
nodes.statement: Using the Baire Category Theorem one can show that there exists $L>1$ such that, if we restrict to a compact set, then the distance $d$ is $L$-biLipschitz invariant, see \cite[Lemma 6.7]{LeDonne1}.
assumptions: if we restrict to a compact set
conclusions: there exists $L>1$ such that, if we restrict to a compact set, then the distance $d$ is $L$-biLipschitz invariant

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: Since $ d_{cc}$ is biLipschitz equivalent to the box distance, up to multiplying $d$ by a constant we assume that $d \le d_{b}$. Using the Baire Category Theorem one can show that there exists $L>1$ such that, if we restrict to a compact set, then the distance $d$ is $L$-biLipschitz invariant, see \cite[Lemma 6.7]{LeDonne1}. Suppose that the claim of the theorem is not true. Hence, by the left-biLipschitz invariance of the distances, for all $N\in \N $ there exists a point $p \in B_{d_b}(0,\frac1{2N})$ with $d_b(0,p) > LN d(0,p)$. Write $r_N := d_b(0,p)>0$. We claim that we have that \begin{eqnarray} \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N) \subset B_d(0,2 r_N) . \end{eqnarray}� Indeed, if $q\in B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$, for some $n\leq N$, then \begin{eqnarray*} d(0,q) & \leq &d(0,p) + d(p,p^2)+\ldots + d(p^{n-1} , p^n) + d(p^n , q)\\ &\leq & LN d(0,p) + d_b(p^n , q) \\ &\leq & d_b(0,p) + r_N/2 < 2r_N. \end{eqnarray*} Moreover, for $i < j<N$, we have that \[ d_b(p^i,p^j) = d_b(0,p^{j-i}) \geq d_b(0,p) = r_N. \] Let $\{q_i\}_{i \in I_N}$ be a maximal $4r_N$-separated net of points with respect to distance $d$ in $B_{d_b}(0,1)$. First, by \eqref{ciccio} for all $i \in I_N$ we have that $ \{B_{d_b}(q_i p^n,\frac12 r_N) \}_{n=0}^{N} $ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $ B_{d_b}(q_i,2r_N) $. Second, $\{B_d(q_i,2r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $B_{d_b}(0,2)$. Hence \[ \#I_N N \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N)) \leq \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2)) . \] Since $\{B_d(q_i,8r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ covers $B_{d_b}(0,1)$, by definition of Hausdorff measure we deduce \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal{H}_d^4(B_{d_b}(0,1)) & \le & \liminf_{N \to \infty} \#I_N (16r_N)^4\\ &\le& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2))}{N\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N))} (16r_N)^4\\ & =& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{64^4}{N} = 0. \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts the assumption $\H^4_{d}(B_{d_b}(0,1))> 0$.
nodes.statement_short: If the conclusion failed, powers $p^n$ of a bad point would pack $N$ disjoint $d_b$-balls into a $d$-ball, forcing $\H^4_d(B_{d_b}(0,1)) = 0$.

nodes.name: Set up the contradiction
nodes.statement: Suppose that the claim of the theorem is not true. Hence, by the left-biLipschitz invariance of the distances, for all $N\in \N $ there exists a point $p \in B_{d_b}(0,\frac1{2N})$ with $d_b(0,p) > LN d(0,p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Negating the conclusion gives, for each $N$, a point $p$ with $d_b(0,p) > LNd(0,p)$.

nodes.name: Pack $N$ powers of $p$ into a small $d$-ball
nodes.statement: Write $r_N := d_b(0,p)>0$. We claim that we have that \begin{eqnarray} \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N) \subset B_d(0,2 r_N) . \end{eqnarray}� Indeed, if $q\in B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$, for some $n\leq N$, then \begin{eqnarray*} d(0,q) & \leq &d(0,p) + d(p,p^2)+\ldots + d(p^{n-1} , p^n) + d(p^n , q)\\ &\leq & LN d(0,p) + d_b(p^n , q) \\ &\leq & d_b(0,p) + r_N/2 < 2r_N. \end{eqnarray*} Moreover, for $i < j<N$, we have that \[ d_b(p^i,p^j) = d_b(0,p^{j-i}) \geq d_b(0,p) = r_N. \]
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping along $p, p^2, \dots, p^N$ shows all the balls $B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$ lie in $B_d(0,2r_N)$ and are disjoint.

nodes.name: Count via a separated net
nodes.statement: Let $\{q_i\}_{i \in I_N}$ be a maximal $4r_N$-separated net of points with respect to distance $d$ in $B_{d_b}(0,1)$. First, by \eqref{ciccio} for all $i \in I_N$ we have that $ \{B_{d_b}(q_i p^n,\frac12 r_N) \}_{n=0}^{N} $ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $ B_{d_b}(q_i,2r_N) $. Second, $\{B_d(q_i,2r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $B_{d_b}(0,2)$. Hence \[ \#I_N N \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N)) \leq \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2)) . \]
nodes.statement_short: A maximal $4r_N$-separated net gives $\#I_N \cdot N \cdot \H^4_{d_b}(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N)) \le \H^4_{d_b}(B_{d_b}(0,2))$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\H^4_d(B_{d_b}(0,1)) = 0$
nodes.statement: Since $\{B_d(q_i,8r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ covers $B_{d_b}(0,1)$, by definition of Hausdorff measure we deduce \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal{H}_d^4(B_{d_b}(0,1)) & \le & \liminf_{N \to \infty} \#I_N (16r_N)^4\\ &\le& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2))}{N\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N))} (16r_N)^4\\ & =& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{64^4}{N} = 0. \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts the assumption $\H^4_{d}(B_{d_b}(0,1))> 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The covering estimate gives $\liminf 64^4/N = 0$, contradicting positivity.

nodes.name: Construction of the left-invariant distance $d_1$
nodes.statement: The distance $d_1$ is defined via \eqref{eq:ddef}. The initial distance is $d_{cc}$ and the shortcuts are defined by first taking a sequence of shortcuts from the origin to points in the vertical direction and then left-translating the shortcuts to start from every point of the space. Since we want none of the tangents to admit nontrivial dilations, we have to be careful in defining the sequence of shortcuts. Let us define the set of shortcuts from the origin as \[ \S_0 = \left\{ \left(0,(0,0,4^{-n}) \right) \;:\; n \in a^{-1}(\{1\}) \right\}, \] where $a \colon \N \to \{0,1\}$ is a function determining whether a shortcut is taken on scale $4^{-n}$. If we were to take $a(n) = 1$ for all $n$, then the tangents would be self-similar. The full set of shortcuts is then defined as \[ \S = \left\{ (p q_1, p q_2 )\; : \; p \in \mathbb H , \,(q_1,q_2) \vee (q_2, q_1) \in \S_0 \right\} \] and the cost function $c \colon \mathbb H \times \mathbb H \to [0,\infty)$ for $(p,q) \in \S$ as \[ c(p,q) = \frac12 d_{cc}(p,q). \] The distance $d_1$ is then defined as the $d$ in \eqref{eq:ddef}. Since $\frac12 d_{cc} \le d_1 \le d_{cc}$, the function $d_1$ is a distance and it is biLipschitz equivalent with $d_{cc}$. By the left-invariace of the set of shortcuts $\S$, the distance $d_1$ is also left-invariant. Since we want to avoid self-similarity, we define the function $a$ so that every word written in the alphabets $\{0,1\}$ appears consecutively in the sequence $(a(n))_{n\in\N}$ only some limited number of times. This is achieved for example by defining \[ a(i) := \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if there exists }k \text{ odd and }l \in \N\text{ such that }i = (k\ell\prod_{h < \ell}p_h+1)p_\ell\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \] where $p_\ell$ is the $\ell$:th prime number.
nodes.statement_short: Take vertical shortcuts from the origin at the scales $4^{-n}$ selected by an aperiodic $0/1$ sequence $a$, left-translate them everywhere, and halve their $d_{cc}$-cost.
input: where $a \colon \N \to \{0,1\}$ is a function determining whether a shortcut is taken on scale $4^{-n}$
output: The distance $d_1$ is then defined as the $d$ in \eqref{eq:ddef}.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.1 (the sequence $a$ never repeats along an arithmetic progression)
nodes.statement: Let $\ell \geq 1$. There exists some $m \geq 1$ so that for any $i \geq 1$, there exists some $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $a(j) \neq a(j+m\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: For each $\ell$ there is $m$ so that every window of length $m\ell$ contains a $j$ with $a(j) \neq a(j+m\ell)$.
assumptions: Let $\ell \geq 1$.
conclusions: There exists some $m \geq 1$ so that for any $i \geq 1$, there exists some $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $a(j) \neq a(j+m\ell)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Let us write \[ P_\ell = \left\{(k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell \,:\, k \in \N\right\}. \] We claim that $\{P_\ell\}_{\ell \in \N}$ is a disjointed collection of sets. In order to see this take $0 < \ell < \ell'< \infty$ and notice that on one hand for every $k \in \N$ we have $p_\ell \mid (k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell$. On the other hand, since $p_\ell \mid \prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}$, we have $p_\ell \nmid (k\ell'\prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}+1)p_{\ell'}$ for all $k \in \N$. Now let $\ell \geq 1$ be given. Define $m = \prod_{h \le \ell}p_{h}$. Then $P_\ell = \{p_\ell + m\ell k \,:\, k \in \N\}$. Let $i \ge 1$ and select $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $j \equiv p_\ell \pmod{m\ell}$. Then by definition, $j \in P_\ell$. By the fact that the sets $P_{\ell'}$ are pairwise disjoint we have from the definition of $a$ that \[ a(m\ell k + p_{\ell}) = \begin{cases} 1,& \text{if }k \text{ is odd},\\ 0,& \text{if }k \text{ is even}. \end{cases} \] Thus $a(j) \neq a(j + \ell m)$.
nodes.statement_short: The sets $P_\ell$ are pairwise disjoint by divisibility by $p_\ell$; taking $m = \prod_{h \le \ell}p_h$ makes $a$ alternate along $P_\ell$.

nodes.statement: Now let $\ell \geq 1$ be given. Define $m = \prod_{h \le \ell}p_{h}$. Then $P_\ell = \{p_\ell + m\ell k \,:\, k \in \N\}$. Let $i \ge 1$ and select $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $j \equiv p_\ell \pmod{m\ell}$. Then by definition, $j \in P_\ell$. nodes.statement_short: On $P_\ell$ the value of $a$ alternates with the parity of $k$.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.3 (uniform lower bound for $d_1$ with a continuous factor $f$)
nodes.statement: There exists a continuous function $f \colon [1,4] \to [\frac12,1]$ with the properties that $f(t)>\frac12$ for all $t \in (1,4)$ and \begin{equation} d_1(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) \ge f(t) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) \end{equation} for all $n \in \N$ and $t \in (1,4)$.
nodes.statement_short: There is a continuous $f$ with $f > 1/2$ on $(1,4)$ such that $d_1(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) \ge f(t)\,d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n}))$.
assumptions: for all $n \in \N$ and $t \in (1,4)$
conclusions: There exists a continuous function $f \colon [1,4] \to [\frac12,1]$ with the properties that $f(t)>\frac12$ for all $t \in (1,4)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.3
nodes.statement: We claim that \[ f(t) = \min \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} , \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ \frac{2t}{t+1}} \right) \] works. It is immediate from definition that $f(t) > 1/2$ for $t \in (1,4)$. Let $\x = (x_0,x_1,\dots,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $0$ to $(0,0,t 4^{-n})$ where $t \in (1,4)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:vertical-itinerary}, we may suppose that $x_{i+1}^{-1}x_i \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$. Let $\ell_k$ be the absolute value of the $z$-coordinate of $x_k^{-1}x_{k-1}$. Let $\ell_M$ be the maximum of the $\ell_k$'s. Then we have that \begin{equation} \sum \ell_k \geq t 4^{-n}. \end{equation} Suppose first that $\ell_M \geq 4^{-n+1}$, then \[ c(\x) \geq \frac{1}{2} \ell_M^{1/2} \geq 2^{-n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n}\geq f(t) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \] and we are done. Thus we have that \[ 2 c(\x) \geq \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{\frac{2}{t+1}} 2^n \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k \overset{\eqref{e:dk-lower}}{\geq} \sqrt{ \frac{2t}{t+1}} \sqrt{t}2^{-n}, \] and we are done.

nodes.name: Case $\ell_M \ge 4^{-n+1}$
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $\ell_M \geq 4^{-n+1}$, then \[ c(\x) \geq \frac{1}{2} \ell_M^{1/2} \geq 2^{-n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n}\geq f(t) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \] and we are done. Then suppose $\ell_M \in \left[ \frac{1+t}{2} 4^{-n}, 4^{-n+1} \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: A very large increment already costs at least $2^{-n}$.

nodes.name: Case $\ell_M$ intermediate
nodes.statement: Then as $t \in (1,4)$, we get that $(x_{M-1},x_{M}) \notin \S$. This gives \[ c(\x) \geq \ell_M^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{ \frac{1+t}{2} } 2^{-n} \geq \sqrt{\frac{1 + t}{2t}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n} \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\sqrt{t}2^{-n}, \] and we are done.

nodes.name: Case $\ell_M$ small
nodes.statement: Finally, suppose that $\ell_M < \frac{1+t}{2} 4^{-n}$. By maximality of $\ell_M$ we then have $\ell_k < \frac{1+t}{2} 4^{-n}$ for all $k$. Thus we have that \[ 2 c(\x) \geq \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{\frac{2}{t+1}} 2^n \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k \overset{\eqref{e:dk-lower}}{\geq} \sqrt{ \frac{2t}{t+1}} \sqrt{t}2^{-n},
nodes.statement_short: All increments small: use concavity of the square root over the sum.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.4 (lower bound $1/\sqrt3$ at unselected scales)
nodes.statement: For all $n \in a^{-1}(\{0\})$ and $t \in (\frac{1}{2},2)$, we have that \begin{equation} d_1(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At scales $n$ where no shortcut is taken, $d_1 \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt3}d_{cc}$ for vertical displacements $t4^{-n}$ with $t \in (\frac12,2)$.
assumptions: For all $n \in a^{-1}(\{0\})$ and $t \in (\frac{1}{2},2)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.4
nodes.statement: The proof is largely analogous to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1}. Let $(x_0,x_1,\dots,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $0$ to $(0,0,t 4^{-n})$ where $t \in (1/2,2)$ and assume that $a(n) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:vertical-itinerary}, we may suppose that $x_{i+1}^{-1}x_i \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$. Let $\ell_k$ and $\ell_M$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1}, so that we have \eqref{e:dk-lower}. Suppose first that $\ell \geq 4^{-n+1}$, then \[ c(\x) \geq \frac{1}{2} \ell^{1/2} \geq 2^{-n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n} \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \] and we are done. Then suppose $\ell \in \left[ \frac{1+4t}{8} 4^{-n}, 4^{-n+1} \right)$. Then as $t \in (1/2,2)$ and $a(n) = 0$, we get that $(x_{M-1},x_M) \notin \S$. This gives \[ c(\x) \geq \ell^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{ \frac{1+4t}{8} } 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n}, \] and we are done. Finally, suppose that $\ell < \frac{1+4t}{8} 4^{-n}$. Thus, we have that $\ell_k < \frac{1+4t}{8} 4^{-n}$ for all $k$. Therefore \begin{equation} 2c(\x) \geq \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{\frac{8}{4t+1}} 2^n \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k \overset{\eqref{e:dk-lower}}{\geq} \sqrt{ \frac{8t^2}{4t+1}} 2^{-n} \ge \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{t}2^{-n}, \end{equation} and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Same three-case analysis as Lemma 6.3, using $a(n)=0$ to rule out the level $n$ shortcut in the middle case.

nodes.name: Reduce to vertical increments
nodes.statement: The proof is largely analogous to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1}. Let $(x_0,x_1,\dots,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $0$ to $(0,0,t 4^{-n})$ where $t \in (1/2,2)$ and assume that $a(n) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:vertical-itinerary}, we may suppose that $x_{i+1}^{-1}x_i \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$. nodes.name: Case $\ell \ge 4^{-n+1}$
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $\ell \geq 4^{-n+1}$, then \[ c(\x) \geq \frac{1}{2} \ell^{1/2} \geq 2^{-n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n} \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \] and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Large increment: direct estimate.

nodes.name: Case $\ell$ intermediate uses $a(n)=0$
nodes.statement: Then suppose $\ell \in \left[ \frac{1+4t}{8} 4^{-n}, 4^{-n+1} \right)$. Then as $t \in (1/2,2)$ and $a(n) = 0$, we get that $(x_{M-1},x_M) \notin \S$. This gives \[ c(\x) \geq \ell^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{ \frac{1+4t}{8} } 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{t} 2^{-n}, \] and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Since $a(n)=0$ there is no level $n$ shortcut, so the increment is paid in full.

nodes.name: Case $\ell$ small
nodes.statement: Finally, suppose that $\ell < \frac{1+4t}{8} 4^{-n}$. Thus, we have that $\ell_k < \frac{1+4t}{8} 4^{-n}$ for all $k$. Therefore \begin{equation} 2c(\x) \geq \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k^{1/2} \geq \sqrt{\frac{8}{4t+1}} 2^n \sum_{k=1}^N \ell_k \overset{\eqref{e:dk-lower}}{\geq} \sqrt{ \frac{8t^2}{4t+1}} 2^{-n} \ge \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{t}2^{-n}, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: All increments small: concavity of the square root again.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.5 (uniform upper bound at selected scales)
nodes.statement: For every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists some $\eta \in (0,1/2)$ such that if $|t| < \eta$ and $a(n) = 1$, then \[ d_1(0,(0,0,(1+t) 4^{-n})) \leq \left( \frac{1}{2} + \epsilon \right) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t) 4^{-n})). \]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.6
nodes.statement: Assume to the contrary that there exists a sequence $(\lambda_j)_{j \in \N}$, with $\lambda_j \to 0$ such that the distances $$(p,q)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d_1(\delta_{\lambda_j} (p),\delta_{\lambda_j} (q)) $$ converge pointwise to some $\rho$, and the distance $\rho$ is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$. Let us now find a contradiction by using the assumed self-similarity. For this purpose let us first take a point $(0,0,s^2) \in \mathbb H$ appearing as limit of points to which there is a shortcut from the origin. In other words, take \begin{equation} s \in [1,2^4] \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty\overline{\bigcup_{i \geq j} \{\lambda_i^{-1}2^{-4(k+1)}\,:\, k \in \N\}}. \end{equation} Then we indeed have \[ \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda_j^2s^2)) = \frac12d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)), \] since $a(4(k+1))= 1$ for all $k \in \N$. Let us then use the function $f$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} to show that there exists $\ell \in \N$ such that $\lambda = 2^\ell$. Supposing this is not the case, we have $\lambda = t2^\ell$ for some $t \in (1,2)$ and $\ell \in \N$. By \eqref{14598015} $s$ is of the form $s=\lim_{m\to \infty} \lambda_{i_m}^{-1} 2^{-4(k_m+1)}$, with $i_m, k_m\to \infty$. Then, by the continuity of the function $f$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,\lambda^2s^2)) & = &\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &\lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} d_1(0,(0,0, t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2 4^\ell 4^{-4(k_m+1)}\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2)) \\ & \ge& \lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} f\left(t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2\right ) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ &=& f(t^2)\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &f(t^2)\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) > \frac12\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lambda \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) , \end{eqnarray*} contradicting the fact that $\rho$ is self-similar with the dilation $\lambda$. Therefore $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \N$. Now we employ the properties of the function $a$. Let $m \in \N$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}. Since $\rho$ is self-similar with factor $2^\ell$, it is self-similar also with factor $2^{\ell m}$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformupperbound}, we have that there exists some $\eta$ such that $(1+\eta)^N = 4$ for some $N \in \N$ and if $a(n) = 1$, then \begin{equation} d_1(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})) \leq 0.51 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})), \qquad \forall t \in (-\eta,\eta). \end{equation} Take $j_0 \in \N$ such that for all $j \ge j_0$ we have \begin{equation} \frac{\rho(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^ks^2))}{\lambda_j^{-1} d_1(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k\lambda_j^2s^2))} \in \left(1 - \frac{1}{100}, 1 + \frac{1}{100} \right), \end{equation} for all $(i,k) \in \{0,1,\dots,2 m\ell\} \times \{0,\dots,N-1\}$. Let $n \in \Z$ be such that $(\lambda_j s)^2 \in \left[ \frac{1}{2} 4^{-n}, 2 \cdot 4^{-n}\right)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}, we have that there exists some $i \in \{0,\dots,m \ell\}$ such that $a(n+i) \neq a(n+ i + m\ell)$. We may suppose without loss of generality that $a(n+i) = 1$ so $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$. We have that there exists some $k \in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ such that $4^i(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in ((1-\eta) 4^{n+i},(1+\eta) 4^{n+i})$. Thus, because $a(n+i) = 1$, we have that \begin{equation} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \overset{\eqref{e:upperbound} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\leq} 0.52 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{equation} On the other hand, because $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$ and $$4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in \left( \frac{1}{2} 4^{n+i+m\ell}, 2 \cdot 4^{n+i+m\ell} \right),$$ we have that \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) &\overset{\eqref{e:sqrt3-lower} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\geq} &\frac{99}{100} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \\ &\geq& 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k s^2)), \\ &=& 0.55 \cdot 2^{m\ell} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} Then by the self-similarity of $\rho$ with ratio $2^{m\ell}$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) & = & 2^{-m\ell}\rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2))\\ & \ge & 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts \eqref{eq:finalcontra}.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a self-similar blow-up with ratio $\lambda$; Lemma 6.3 forces $\lambda = 2^\ell$, then Lemma 6.1 produces two scales with incompatible upper and lower bounds.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.7
nodes.statement: Let $(a,b) \in D_n$ be so that $(x,y) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ ($\delta$ to be chosen later) and let $\x = (x_0,...,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $(x,y,z)$ to $(x,y,z + t4^{-n})$. nodes.name: Proof that no blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant or self-similar
nodes.statement: Since the shortcuts are horizontally located on the centers of the dyadic cubes, we have from an easy argument using Lemmas \ref{l:off-grid} and \ref{l:grid-upper} that no blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant. In order to see that no blow-up of $d_2$ is self-similar we argue similarly as for the distance $d_1$. First suppose that a blow-up is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$. This time, instead of finding a limit point $(0,0,s^2)$ of shortcuts from the origin, we find by compactness a pair of points $(x,y,z)$, $(x,y,z + s^2)$ in $B_{d_{cc}}(0,2^5)$ with $s \in [1,2^4]$ appearing as the limit of endpoints of a sequence of shortcuts. This is possible after passing to a subsequence because $a(4(n+1)) = 1$ for all $n$. Observe that Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} holds also for $d_2$ since $d_2 \ge d_1$. As in the case of $d_1$, it then follows via Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} that $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \N$. A contradiction with self-similarity then follows again by the properties of the function $a$. This concludes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:fail}.
nodes.statement_short: The on-grid/off-grid contrast of Lemmas 6.7 and 6.8 breaks left-invariance, and the $d_1$ argument transfers to $d_2$ since $d_2 \ge d_1$.
